title: Semi-analytic Inference of Satellite Densities in the Cold Dark Matter Model Part I. Comparison to Ultra-faint Dwarf Kinematics
comment: 22+11 pages, 8+6 figures, video abstract at https://youtu.be/dal8_lRz3EI
summary: Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are critical testing grounds for probing the limits of galaxy formation in the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm. Employing a semi-analytic cosmological satellite generator that captures the expected CDM halo population, we estimate Milky Way dwarf density profiles through two methods: a kinematic approach using stellar velocity dispersions and a separate method based on dwarf stellar masses. The kinematic approach yields a larger diversity in central dark matter densities than expected from the CDM population, as inferred from the stellar-to-halo mass relation, with compact ultra-faints appearing overdense and larger systems appearing underdense. For the ultra-faint dwarfs with at least 10 stars with spectroscopic measurements, this discrepancy persists at the ~2.4$σ$ level across all considered systematic variations on the semi-analytic modeling. Our framework introduces a novel, robust procedure for testing the consistency of the observed population of Milky Way satellites with cosmological expectations. As future surveys discover new dwarf satellites and refine stellar velocity measurements, updating this analysis will provide an increasingly stringent test of the CDM paradigm.

AI.tldr: The paper tests CDM predictions for the Milky Way's ultra-faint dwarf galaxies using a semi-analytic satellite generator. Two methods estimating central dark matter densities—one kinematic (stellar velocity dispersions) and one based on stellar-to-halo mass relations—reveal a ~2.4σ discrepancy: compact ultra-faints appear overdense while larger systems appear underdense relative to CDM expectations.
AI.motivation: Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies probe the limits of galaxy formation in the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm, and their central dark matter densities provide a stringent observational test of whether observed satellites match cosmological expectations.
AI.method: A semi-analytic cosmological satellite generator captures the expected CDM halo population. Milky Way dwarf density profiles are estimated via two independent approaches: (1) a kinematic method using stellar velocity dispersions, and (2) a method based on dwarf stellar masses via the stellar-to-halo mass relation. Systematic variations in the semi-analytic modeling are considered.
AI.result: The kinematic approach yields greater diversity in central dark matter densities than the CDM population predicts: compact ultra-faint dwarfs appear overdense and larger systems appear underdense. For ultra-faint dwarfs with ≥10 spectroscopically measured stars, the discrepancy persists at ~2.4σ across all considered systematic variations.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a novel, robust procedure for testing the consistency of observed Milky Way satellites with cosmological CDM predictions. As future surveys discover more dwarf satellites and improve stellar velocity measurements, updating this analysis will yield increasingly stringent tests of the CDM paradigm.

title: Superdiffusion at the Galactic Centre
summary: Tracking S-star cluster orbits around Sgr A* calibrates orbital transport models for space-borne gravitational wave detectors. Standard kinetic theories model this cluster via local Fokker-Planck equations, which predict that general relativistic precession halts angular momentum diffusion at the Schwarzschild barrier. Because inverse-square gravitational encounters generate a Holtsmark torque distribution with infinite variance, resonant relaxation operates as a space-fractional process governed by non-local Lévy flights. We simulate this superdiffusive continuous-time random walk using a Markov chain initialized with empirical S-star orbits, including the recently observd S301. Integro-differential fractional operators allow trajectories to cross regions of quenched local diffusion without density buildup at the barrier. Non-equilibrium regimes yield immediate linear flux growth, while secular tidal heating at periastron inflates stellar radii to shift disruption boundaries. Regularized backward integration of the fractional transport equation traces current phase space configurations back to initial deposition states, matching the energy requirements of the \emph{Fermi} bubbles. Relativistic precession does not suppress mass-ratio inspiral rates, which provides a model for event topologies in target galactic nuclei.

AI.tldr: This paper models the S-star cluster around Sgr A* using a space-fractional Fokker-Planck (superdiffusive Lévy flight) framework rather than standard local kinetic theory, since resonant relaxation produces infinite-variance torque distributions. Simulating a Markov-chain continuous-time random walk with empirical orbits (including S301), the authors show trajectories can cross the Schwarzschild barrier without density buildup, yield linear flux growth in non-equilibrium regimes, and that tidal heating at periastron shifts disruption boundaries. Backward integration matches the Fermi bubble energy budget, and relativistic precession does not suppress mass-ratio inspiral rates, providing event topology models for galactic nuclei.
AI.motivation: Standard local Fokker-Planck kinetic theories predict that general relativistic precession halts angular momentum diffusion at the Schwarzschild barrier, which may be incorrect. Because gravitational encounters produce a Holtsmark torque distribution with infinite variance, resonant relaxation is inherently non-local and superdiffusive, requiring a fractional transport description to genuinely capture S-star cluster dynamics and calibrate orbital transport models for space-borne gravitational wave detectors.
AI.method: The authors (1) exploit that inverse-square gravitational encounters yield a Holtsmark torque distribution with infinite variance, justifying a space-fractional (Lévy flight) continuous-time random walk model of resonant relaxation; (2) initialize a Markov chain simulation with empirical S-star orbits including the newly observed S301; (3) use integro-differential fractional operators to allow trajectories to cross quenched local-diffusion regions; (4) include secular tidal heating at periastron to inflate stellar radii and shift disruption boundaries; and (5) perform regularized backward integration of the fractional transport equation to map current phase-space configurations to initial deposition states.
AI.result: Trajectories cross the Schwarzschild barrier without density buildup. Non-equilibrium regimes show immediate linear flux growth. Tidal heating at periastron inflates stellar radii, moving disruption boundaries. Backward regularized integration of the fractional transport equation links current phase-space configurations to initial deposition states that match the Fermi bubble energy requirements. Relativistic precession does not suppress mass-ratio inspiral rates, providing a model for event topologies in target galactic nuclei.
AI.conclusion: The space-fractional (superdiffusive) treatment of resonant relaxation accounts for barrier-crossing and inspiral behavior that standard local Fokker-Planck theory cannot, and the resulting fractional transport framework yields predictions for S-star dynamics, tidal disruption, Fermi bubble energetics, and extreme mass-ratio inspiral rates relevant to gravitational wave detectors and target galactic nuclei.

title: The influence of feedback on the baryonic content of haloes in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: We present predictions for the relation between the halo gas mass fraction and halo mass, $f_{\rm gas}^{200}-M_{200}$, from the COLIBRE cosmological simulations of galaxy formation, and explore how the gas content of haloes is influenced by feedback from supernovae and active galactic nuclei (AGN) over time. The $f_{\rm gas}^{200}-M_{200}$ relation in COLIBRE is non-monotonic, with a peak at $M_{200}\sim 10^{11.5-12}$~M$_\odot$. Below this mass, feedback from supernovae efficiently expels gas from the haloes of dwarf galaxies, and above it, AGN feedback efficiently depletes the haloes of galaxy groups. The fiducial COLIBRE model yields gas fractions for galaxy groups and clusters that agree with constraints from Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray data, but which are high relative to gas fractions inferred from eROSITA stacks and measurements of the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel-dovich (kSZ) effect. COLIBRE's hybrid AGN feedback model, which combines thermal and jet-driven feedback, produces lower gas fractions in better agreement with eROSITA and kSZ measurements. COLIBRE produces lower gas fractions for groups and clusters than EAGLE and other contemporary simulations, and better agreement with observational constraints. We investigate the origin of this improvement relative to EAGLE, and how the resolution of the simulation affects the impact of feedback. Our results demonstrate that halo gas fractions are a sensitive probe of feedback physics, and that they can differ significantly between simulations that otherwise produce very similar galaxy populations.

AI.tldr: This paper predicts the halo gas mass fraction–halo mass relation from the COLIBRE cosmological simulations, finding a non-monotonic relation peaking at M200 ~ 10^11.5-12 Msun, shaped by supernova feedback in dwarf halos (lower masses) and AGN feedback in group halos (higher masses). COLIBRE produces lower gas fractions for groups/clusters than EAGLE and other simulations, agreeing better with eROSITA and kSZ measurements when using its hybrid thermal+jet AGN feedback model, demonstrating that halo gas fractions are a sensitive probe of feedback physics.
AI.motivation: To understand how feedback from supernovae and AGN shapes the gas content of dark matter haloes across mass scales and over time, and to assess whether current cosmological simulations can reproduce observational constraints on halo gas fractions from X-ray, X-ray stacking, and kSZ measurements.
AI.method: Using the COLIBRE cosmological simulations of galaxy formation, the authors compute the f_gas^200–M200 relation and compare fiducial and hybrid (thermal + jet-driven) AGN feedback models. They also compare against EAGLE and other contemporary simulations, investigate the origin of improvements relative to EAGLE, and study the resolution dependence of feedback effects.
AI.result: The f_gas^200–M200 relation is non-monotonic, peaking at M200~10^11.5-12 Msun. Supernova feedback expels gas from dwarf halos (lower masses) and AGN feedback depletes group/cluster halos (higher masses). Fiducial COLIBRE matches Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray constraints but overpredicts gas fractions relative to eROSITA stacks and kSZ measurements. The hybrid AGN feedback model yields lower gas fractions in better agreement with eROSITA and kSZ. COLIBRE produces lower group/cluster gas fractions than EAGLE and other contemporary simulations, with better agreement with observations.
AI.conclusion: Halo gas fractions serve as a sensitive diagnostic of feedback physics, and can differ substantially between simulations that otherwise reproduce similar galaxy populations. The hybrid (thermal + jet) AGN feedback scheme in COLIBRE is key to improving agreement with observational gas fraction constraints.

title: An Exploratory Analysis of New Large Gaia-informed Quasar Samples in SDSS-V
comment: Resubmitted to ApJ on 28 July 2026 after addressing the referee report. The data will be available in SDSS-V/DR20
summary: Quasars are luminous objects that provide insights into the physics and evolution of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion flows, galaxy evolution, and even cosmology. In this study, we present an exploratory study based on the ongoing fifth generation of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-V) and its unique dual-hemisphere, wide-field, and multi-object spectroscopic capabilities, with the aim of creating a comprehensive, all-sky quasar sample. The targets were selected through two novel methods, GUA and Skewt-QSO, that rely primarily on data from WISE and Gaia, aiming to address gaps in previous large quasar samples. Our sample includes over 250,000 spectroscopically confirmed quasars reaching z~5, with tens of thousands of newly identified quasars in the southern hemisphere. The selection methods are highly pure, with well over 80% of the spectra collected being genuine quasars; the main contaminants are M-type stars. The detailed spectral decomposition procedure we employed shows that the quasars in the sample span a wide range of luminosities (Lbol~$10^{44}-10^{48} erg s^{-1}$), SMBH masses (MBH~$10^6-10^{10}$ Msun), and accretion rates (L/LEdd~0.01-1). The distributions of these properties are consistent with those of previous quasar catalogs, which are based on past generations of SDSS, once we account for potential selection biases related to the various survey depths. Our findings confirm that novel selection methods based on optical+IR colors and/or astrometry can yield a large, high-purity quasar sample over wide sky areas, including in cases where more nuanced multi-band photometry and/or multi-wavelength data in the X-ray or radio is not available. This SDSS-V sample, which will continue to grow, establishes a robust reference for future southern (time-domain) surveys, while enhancing and complementing our understanding of quasar demographics and SMBH evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an exploratory study using SDSS-V's dual-hemisphere spectroscopic capabilities to build a comprehensive all-sky quasar sample of over 250,000 spectroscopically confirmed quasars (reaching z~5), selected via two novel methods (GUA and Skewt-QSO) based on WISE and Gaia data. The sample is highly pure (>80% genuine quasars), spans a wide range of luminosities, SMBH masses, and accretion rates, and provides a robust reference for future southern time-domain surveys.
AI.motivation: To create a comprehensive, all-sky quasar sample that addresses gaps in previous large quasar samples—particularly the lack of coverage in the southern hemisphere—by leveraging SDSS-V's unique dual-hemisphere, wide-field, multi-object spectroscopic capabilities.
AI.method: Two novel selection methods (GUA and Skewt-QSO) based primarily on WISE and Gaia data (optical+IR colors and astrometry) were used to target quasars across the sky. Spectroscopic confirmation was obtained via SDSS-V, followed by detailed spectral decomposition to derive physical properties including bolometric luminosity, SMBH mass, and Eddington ratios.
AI.result: The sample includes over 250,000 spectroscopically confirmed quasars reaching z~5, with tens of thousands of newly identified quasars in the southern hemisphere. Selection purity exceeds 80% (with M-type stars as the main contaminants). Quasars span Lbol~10^44-10^48 erg/s, MBH~10^6-10^10 Msun, and L/LEdd~0.01-1, with distributions consistent with previous SDSS quasar catalogs after accounting for selection biases.
AI.conclusion: Novel optical+IR color and astrometry-based selection methods can produce large, high-purity quasar samples over wide sky areas, even without X-ray or radio data. This growing SDSS-V sample establishes a robust reference for future southern time-domain surveys and enhances our understanding of quasar demographics and SMBH evolution.

title: Semi-analytic Inference of Satellite Densities in the Cold Dark Matter Model Part II. Implications for Dark Matter Indirect Detection Constraints
comment: 16+9 pages, 4+6 figures, video abstract at https://youtu.be/x9zNkN6XyAA
summary: Dwarf galaxies provide excellent targets to search for signals of dark matter annihilation or decay. Using a calibrated semi-analytic model and the latest stellar kinematic data (presented in Part I), this paper updates the astrophysical J-factors for the Milky Way's dwarf spheroidal galaxies. We infer the probability distributions for the J-factors of 39 dwarfs by conditioning a population of subhalos, generated with the SatGen semi-analytic satellite model, on either a dwarf's kinematically determined dynamical mass or its stellar mass. We also compute the J-factors using the Jeans equation with updated stellar kinematics and priors that incorporate varying degrees of SatGen information. We use the computed J-factors to recast existing limits from Fermi-LAT data on the annihilation cross section. Our main result is that variations in the J-factors computed using the Jeans analysis introduce a factor of 2-4 uncertainty into the inferred limits on the cross section. We argue that a cosmologically informed prior is a motivated choice that excludes thermal relic annihilation cross sections to $b\bar{b}$ below about 70 GeV. For comparison, the more commonly used priors, which can lead to unphysical halo parameters, exclude masses below 130 GeV at 95% confidence level. We also show that the highest-J-factor dwarfs are spatially extended, approximately one degree on the sky, which challenges the validity of the point-source approximation adopted in many analyses of Fermi data. Finally, based on the semi-analytic model and the kinematic data, the highest J-factor halos have already been discovered, suggesting future ultra-faint discoveries are unlikely to substantially strengthen limits on annihilating dark matter.

AI.tldr: This paper updates the astrophysical J-factors for 39 Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies using a calibrated semi-analytic model (SatGen) conditioned on dynamical or stellar masses, combined with Jeans-equation analyses using updated stellar kinematics. It shows that Jeans-based J-factor variations introduce factor 2-4 uncertainty in Fermi-LAT annihilation cross-section limits, that cosmologically informed priors exclude thermal relic annihilation to b-bbar below ~70 GeV (vs ~130 GeV with common priors), that the highest-J dwarfs are spatially extended (challenging point-source approximations), and that the highest-J halos have already been discovered.
AI.motivation: Dwarf galaxies are prime targets for dark matter annihilation/decay searches. Accurate J-factors (astrophysical factors governing the DM signal strength) are critical for correctly interpreting gamma-ray search limits, yet previous determinations suffered from uncertain halo profiles and limited kinematic data. This paper aims to produce more robust J-factor estimates by combining a physically motivated semi-analytic model of subhalo populations with the latest stellar kinematic data, thereby improving the reliability of dark matter constraints from gamma-ray observations.
AI.method: The authors use a calibrated semi-analytic satellite model (SatGen) to generate a population of subhalos and infer J-factor probability distributions for 39 dwarfs by conditioning the subhalo population on either kinematically determined dynamical masses or stellar masses. They also compute J-factors using the Jeans equation with updated stellar kinematics from Part I, incorporating priors that inject varying degrees of SatGen information. The resulting J-factors are used to recast existing Fermi-LAT annihilation cross-section limits.
AI.result: Jeans-based J-factor variations introduce a factor of 2-4 uncertainty in inferred cross-section limits. A cosmologically informed prior excludes thermal relic annihilation cross sections to b-bbar below about 70 GeV, whereas more commonly used priors (which can yield unphysical halo parameters) exclude masses below 130 GeV at 95% confidence. The highest-J-factor dwarfs are spatially extended (~1 degree on sky), challenging the point-source approximation used in many Fermi analyses. Additionally, the highest-J halos have already been discovered, so future ultra-faint dwarf discoveries are unlikely to substantially strengthen annihilation limits.
AI.conclusion: Cosmologically motivated priors are a more physically sound choice for J-factor inference, yielding softer (more conservative) exclusion limits on dark matter annihilation. The spatial extension of high-J dwarfs calls for extended-source analyses of Fermi data rather than point-source approximations, and the discovery-space for high-J dwarfs is essentially saturated, meaning improved limits will require better data or methods rather than new dwarf discoveries.

title: Exploring the Limits of Spectral Line Stacking in Spectral Line Data and Application Toward the Detection of Bulk $^{13}$C Enrichment of Aromatics in TMC-1
summary: The formation history of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the interstellar medium remains a topic of active debate, with proposed mechanisms ranging from high-temperature stellar ejecta processes to low-temperature chemistry within molecular clouds. Recently, the identification of small PAHs in the cold, dark cloud TMC-1 has provided some circumstantial evidence of the latter. If these are formed in situ, their isotopic ratios, particularly $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, should reflect the local, bulk material of the molecular cloud; in contrast, PAHs formed in the circumstellar envelopes of evolved stars may show enhanced $^{13}$C abundances. The expected radio signals of these $^{13}$C substituted species will be faint, and thus we conducted a detailed proof-of-concept analysis examining whether spectral line stacking and matched filtering techniques can robustly retrieve signal from multiple singly substituted $^{13}$C isotopologues in aggregate. We find that while retrieved signal decreases in the limit of spectral line confusion, false-positive detections are exceedingly improbable at the adopted 5$σ$ matched filter response detection threshold. We then demonstrate the technique on actual observational data of isotopologues of HC$_9$N toward TMC-1. Finally, we show using synthetic data that if laboratory rotational spectra of all singly substituted $^{13}$C isotopologues of cyanonaphthalene and cyanopyrene isomers existed, current observations of TMC-1 would be sensitive enough to discriminate between a local, bulk $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio and one with an enhanced $^{13}$C abundance suggestive of inheritance.

AI.tldr: This paper explores whether PAHs in cold molecular clouds like TMC-1 form in situ or are inherited from evolved stars, using 13C/12C isotopic ratios as a discriminant. The authors perform a proof-of-concept analysis showing that spectral line stacking and matched filtering can robustly detect faint signals from multiple singly substituted 13C isotopologues, demonstrate the technique on HC9N isotopologues toward TMC-1, and use synthetic data to show that existing TMC-1 observations could discriminate between a local bulk 12C/13C ratio and an enhanced 13C abundance suggestive of stellar inheritance, if laboratory spectra of key PAH isotopologues existed.
AI.motivation: The formation history of PAHs in the interstellar medium is debated, with competing scenarios of high-temperature stellar ejecta processes versus low-temperature molecular cloud chemistry. The recent detection of small PAHs in the cold dark cloud TMC-1 provides circumstantial evidence for in situ formation, and isotopic ratios (12C/13C) of PAHs could discriminate between local formation (reflecting bulk cloud material) and inherited formation (showing enhanced 13C from evolved stars).
AI.method: The authors conduct a proof-of-concept analysis using spectral line stacking and matched filtering techniques to retrieve faint signals from multiple singly substituted 13C isotopologues in aggregate. They assess signal retrieval in the limit of spectral line confusion and evaluate false-positive rates at a 5σ matched filter detection threshold. The technique is demonstrated on actual observational data of HC9N isotopologues toward TMC-1, and synthetic data are used to test whether current observations could distinguish local vs. inherited 13C enrichment for cyanonaphthalene and cyanopyrene isomers.
AI.result: Retrieved signal decreases in the limit of spectral line confusion, but false-positive detections are exceedingly improbable at the adopted 5σ matched filter detection threshold. The technique is successfully demonstrated on real HC9N isotopologue observations toward TMC-1. Synthetic data show that if laboratory rotational spectra of all singly substituted 13C isotopologues of cyanonaphthalene and cyanopyrene existed, current TMC-1 observations would be sensitive enough to discriminate between a local bulk 12C/13C ratio and an enhanced 13C abundance suggestive of inheritance.
AI.conclusion: Spectral line stacking and matched filtering offer a viable path to measuring 12C/13C isotopic ratios in small PAHs in cold clouds. Such measurements could distinguish between in situ molecular cloud formation and inheritance from evolved stellar sources, though the necessary laboratory rotational spectra for key PAH isotopologues (e.g., cyanonaphthalene and cyanopyrene) remain a prerequisite for the full application of this diagnostic.

title: Relativistic effects of PSR~J1856--0039 double neutron star system in a 2.36-hour compact orbit
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, accepted by Phys. Rev. Lett
summary: Compact double neutron star (DNS) systems are unique laboratories for testing gravitational theories and studying DNS mergers. Here we report the properties of a new DNS system, PSR J1856--0039, discovered in the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). The pulsar is mildly recycled with a period of 23.4~ms in a compact eccentric orbit ($e=0.106$) with an orbital period of 2.36 hours. By following up FAST observations, we measured the relativistic effects, including the orbital period derivative $\dot{P}_{\rm orb}=-1.284\pm0.019\times10^{-12}$ s s$^{-1}$, periastron advance $\dotω=17.5859\pm0.0007$ deg yr$^{-1}$, and Einstein delay $γ=0.445\pm0.011$ ms. This DNS system has a low orbital inclination of $i=133^\circ.2\pm1^\circ.1$ and the lowest total mass of any known DNS, $M_{\rm tot}=2.48841\pm0.00015 M\odot$, with a determined pulsar mass of $1.304\pm0.022 M_\odot$ and a companion mass of $1.185\pm0.022 M_\odot$, one of the lowest neutron-star masses. The observed orbital decay due to gravitational-wave emission $\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,obs}$ and the orbital decay predicted by general relativity $\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,pred}$ are consistent at a level of $\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,obs}/\dot{P}^{\rm GW}_{\rm orb,pred}=$1.009(14) (68% confidence). This DNS will merge after 82 Myr and may form a stable neutron star or collapse into a black hole after spin-down. Long-term monitoring could potentially probe the Lense-Thirring precession.

AI.tldr: PSR J1856-0039 is a new compact double neutron star system discovered with FAST, featuring a mildly recycled 23.4 ms pulsar in a 2.36-hour eccentric orbit. It has the lowest total mass of any known DNS (2.48841 M_sun), a low orbital inclination, and a remarkably low neutron-star companion mass (1.185 M_sun). General relativity precisely predicts the observed orbital decay from gravitational-wave emission, confirming GR, and the system will merge in ~82 Myr.
AI.motivation: DNS systems serve as unique laboratories for testing gravitational theories and understanding DNS merger outcomes. Discovering new DNS systems with extreme parameter values allows stringent tests of general relativity and insights into neutron-star formation and evolution.
AI.method: Discovery and follow-up observations using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). Relativistic timing parameters (orbital period derivative, periastron advance, Einstein delay) were measured to determine system masses, orbital geometry, and test GR predictions of gravitational-wave-driven orbital decay.
AI.result: The system has the lowest total mass of any known DNS at 2.48841±0.00015 M_sun, with pulsar mass 1.304±0.022 M_sun and companion mass 1.185±0.022 M_sun (one of the lowest neutron-star masses). The ratio of observed to predicted GW-driven orbital decay is 1.009(14), consistent with general relativity. The merger time is ~82 Myr. The low inclination (i=133.2°) enables potentially probing Lense-Thirring precession via long-term monitoring.
AI.conclusion: PSR J1856-0039 provides a new, stringent test of general relativity in the strong-field regime, agrees with GR predictions of gravitational-wave emission, and offers a unique system for studying neutron-star mass extremes and DNS merger outcomes. Future long-term monitoring could probe Lense-Thirring precession.

title: Cosmic Pairs: A DESI Census of Dual and Offset AGN as Precursors to Massive Black Hole Binaries
comment: 38 pages, 18 figures, 1 table. To be submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a systematic census of dual and offset active galactic nuclei (AGN) using spectroscopic data from the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). After correcting for observational systematics, our final sample contains $>7,000$ dual AGN and 27,000 galaxy pairs containing one AGN over the redshift range $0 \lesssim z \lesssim 3.6$. This sample expands the known dual AGN sample by $\sim 1-2$ orders of magnitude at $0.2 \lesssim z \lesssim 0.4$, includes $\sim 50$ dwarf dual AGN candidates in a regime where only a handful were previously known, and triples the census at $z>2$. Dual AGN are preferentially found at small separations, consistent with merger-driven triggering of AGN activity. The two members of a pair differ in their star formation response: the more massive (primary) host changes little with separation, while the less massive (secondary) lies $\sim 0.3$ dex above matched inactive and one-AGN companions at the same projected separation in main-sequence offset. Using ASTRID simulations, we predict that the fraction of DESI dual AGN whose central black holes will merge by $z \sim 0$ increases with redshift, reaching $\sim 76\%$ by $z \sim 2$, while the fraction producing LISA-detectable mergers peaks at $\sim 37\%$ near $z \sim 0.9$. These results provide the largest uniformly selected spectroscopic sample of kpc-scale dual and offset AGN candidates from a single survey, connecting their host-galaxy and AGN demographics to the progenitor population of massive black hole mergers detectable by LISA.

This expands the known dual AGN sample by 1-2 orders of magnitude at moderate redshifts, includes ~50 dwarf dual AGN candidates, and triples the census at z>2. Using ASTRID simulations, they predict merger fractions reaching ~76% for central black hole mergers by z~0 and ~37% LISA-detectable mergers near z~0.9.
AI.motivation: Dual AGN are key probes of merger-driven AGN triggering and represent the progenitor population of massive black hole mergers detectable by LISA. Previous samples were extremely limited in size, particularly in the dwarf regime and at high redshift, motivating a large, uniformly selected spectroscopic census.
AI.method: The authors use spectroscopic data from DESI DR1 to identify dual and offset AGN, applying corrections for observational systematics. They analyze the demographics of the resulting sample, comparing star formation properties of primary vs. secondary hosts, and use ASTRID simulations to project the fraction of these systems whose black holes will eventually merge and be detectable by LISA.
AI.result: The final sample contains >7,000 dual AGN and 27,000 one-AGN pairs. Dual AGN are preferentially found at small separations, consistent with merger-driven triggering. The secondary host lies ~0.3 dex above matched inactive/one-AGN companions in main-sequence offset, while the primary shows little change with separation. ASTRID predicts ~76% of central black holes from DESI dual AGN merge by z~0 (highest at z~2), with LISA-detectable mergers peaking at ~37% near z~0.9.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the largest uniformly selected spectroscopic sample of kpc-scale dual and offset AGN candidates from a single survey, connecting host-galaxy and AGN demographics to the progenitor population of massive black hole mergers detectable by LISA.

title: Exploring cosmic magnetism with gamma-ray burst afterglow emission
summary: The nature and origin of magnetic fields on cosmological scales are still unclear. Magnetic fields detected in galaxies and galaxy clusters are typically interpreted as the result of the amplification of weak seed fields, but their nature remains largely unknown with two scenarios considered: the cosmological and the astrophysical origin. Signatures of magnetization in cosmic voids from observations of very high energy (VHE, E > 100 GeV) photons from extragalactic sources can provide crucial results. Indeed, if a non-negligible intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF) is present in the voids, a time-delayed emission known as pair-echo is expected. The timing and intensity of this signal encode information on the IGMF strength B and properties. Given the recent detection of GRB afterglows at TeV energies, in this article we perform a detectability study of pair-echo signatures from GRBs. We simulate afterglow emission for different values of the jet kinetic energy (E$_{k,iso}$ = 10$^{49}$ - 10$^{55}$ erg), redshift (z = 0.03 - 1), and lightcurve break times, and estimate the expected pair-echo radiation for IGMF strengths in the range B = 10$^{-19}$ - 10$^{-16}$ G. We investigate the capability of CTAO to detect the resulting emission at tens of GeV. We find that a subsample of GRBs in the z - E$_{k,iso}$ parameter space can produce a detectable pair-echo component for CTAO for all the tested IGMF strengths. A steepening of the GRB afterglow light curve, caused e.g. by an early (0.1 - 1 days) jet break, is a key factor to increase the chances of detection. CTAO observations starting from 10 - 12 hrs up to a few days after the GRB trigger time can provide relevant results to probe IGMF.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the detectability of pair-echo signatures from gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) using the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO), simulating afterglow emission across a range of jet kinetic energies, redshifts, and intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF) strengths to assess whether pair-echo emission can be observed and used to probe the nature of cosmological magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: The nature and origin of magnetic fields on cosmological scales remain unknown. Detecting signatures of magnetization in cosmic voids through pair-echo emission from GRBs can provide crucial constraints on the intergalactic magnetic field (IGMF), distinguishing between cosmological and astrophysical origin scenarios. The recent detection of GRB afterglows at TeV energies motivates investigating whether next-generation instruments can detect these pair-echo signals.
AI.method: The authors simulate GRB afterglow emission for a range of parameters: jet kinetic energy (E_k,iso = 10^49 - 10^55 erg), redshift (z = 0.03 - 1), and lightcurve break times. They estimate the expected pair-echo radiation for IGMF strengths ranging from B = 10^-19 to 10^-16 G, and investigate the capability of CTAO to detect the resulting emission at tens of GeV energies.
AI.result: A subsample of GRBs in the z - E_k,iso parameter space can produce a detectable pair-echo component for CTAO across all tested IGMF strengths. A steepening of the GRB afterglow light curve, e.g., caused by an early (0.1 - 1 days) jet break, significantly increases detection chances. CTAO observations starting from 10-12 hours up to a few days after trigger are promising.
AI.conclusion: CTAO observations of GRB afterglows started 10-12 hours up to a few days after trigger can provide relevant results to probe the IGMF and thus constrain the origin of cosmological magnetic fields, particularly for GRBs with early jet breaks that produce detectable pair-echo components.

title: Stellar photoionisation modelling in SYNTHESIZER
comment: 29 pages and 29 figures. Submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: Emission from photoionised gas surrounding young stellar populations ($H\text{II}$ regions) provides critical diagnostics of the physical conditions in star forming galaxies. This emission constrains the gas properties, the nature of ionising sources, and generates essential features for determining galaxy redshifts. To leverage spectroscopic observations to test galaxy formation models, it is essential to incorporate these emissions into synthetic datasets. Here, we present the integration of photoionised gas emission into the SYNTHESIZER package (https://synthesizer-project.github.io) and demonstrate its application. We quantify the impact of key modelling assumptions - including stellar population synthesis models, initial mass functions, ionisation parameter, gas density, geometry, abundance pattern, elemental depletion, and dust - on spectral diagnostics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of SYNTHESIZER through its application in different scenarios ranging from exploring emission in toy parametric models to large-volume cosmological simulations with realistic star formation and metal enrichment histories. Taken together, SYNTHESIZER provides a flexible, physically motivated framework to model stellar and nebular emissions, serving as a vital link between theory and observations in the era of next-generation spectroscopic missions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the integration of photoionised gas (HII region) emission into the SYNTHESIZER package, a flexible Python framework for modelling stellar and nebular emissions in galaxies, and demonstrates its application across toy models and cosmological simulations.
AI.motivation: Emission from photoionised gas surrounding young stellar populations provides critical diagnostics for physical conditions in star-forming galaxies and essential features for redshift determination. To test galaxy formation models with spectroscopic observations, these emissions must be incorporated into synthetic datasets.
AI.method: Integration of photoionised gas emission into the SYNTHESIZER package, quantifying the impact of key modelling assumptions including stellar population synthesis models, initial mass functions, ionisation parameter, gas density, geometry, abundance pattern, elemental depletion, and dust on spectral diagnostics. Applications range from toy parametric models to large-volume cosmological simulations with realistic star formation and metal enrichment histories.
AI.result: SYNTHESIZER provides a flexible, physically motivated framework that models both stellar and nebular emissions, quantifies the effects of various modelling assumptions on spectral diagnostics, and demonstrates versatility across different application scenarios from simple parametric models to full cosmological simulations.
AI.conclusion: SYNTHESIZER serves as a vital link between theory and observations, providing a comprehensive framework for modelling stellar and nebular emissions in the era of next-generation spectroscopic missions.

title: Binary neutron star populations across cosmic time: the impact of binary stellar evolution uncertainties
summary: We investigate the impact of uncertainties in binary stellar evolution on the formation efficiency and cosmological merger rate of BNS systems. In particular, we aim to determine whether robust signatures of binary evolution can be identified across a broad range of metallicities. We perform a systematic exploration of 72 binary evolution models using the population synthesis code COSMIC. We vary four key parameters controlling the onset and efficiency of common-envelope evolution, the natal kick prescription, and the treatment of kicks during the common envelope phase. For each model, we compute the BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rate using several prescriptions for the cosmic metallicity-redshift relation. We identify characteristic features in the metallicity dependence of the BNS formation efficiency that arise from specific evolutionary processes. These include the onset of first-giant-branch skipping at low metallicity and a non-monotonic evolution between $Z=10^{-3}$ and $7.5\times 10^{-3}$. All models also predict a bimodal distribution of BNS progenitor masses associated with two distinct formation channels. The common envelope ejection efficiency and natal kick prescription remain the dominant sources of uncertainty, producing variations of several orders of magnitude in both the BNS formation efficiency and the cosmological merger rate. Finally, we show that different combinations of binary-evolution parameters can produce similar merger-rate histories, highlighting significant degeneracies among population-synthesis models. Current gravitational-wave observations can rule out only the least efficient formation scenarios. Breaking these degeneracies will require larger samples of BNS mergers expected from future third-generation gravitational-wave observatories, and improved observational constraints on the evolution of metallicity across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: The paper explores 72 binary stellar evolution models using the COSMIC population synthesis code, systematically varying key parameters (common-envelope efficiency, natal kicks, and kick treatment during CE) to study BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rates across metallicities. It identifies characteristic metallicity-dependent features, a bimodal progenitor mass distribution, and dominant uncertainties from CE efficiency and natal kicks—which cause order-of-magnitude variations. Significant parameter degeneracies limit current GW observations to ruling out only the least efficient scenarios, necessitating third-generation detectors and better metallicity evolution constraints.
AI.motivation: To determine whether robust signatures of binary stellar evolution can be identified across a broad range of metallicities and to assess how binary evolution uncertainties impact BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rates.
AI.method: Systematic population synthesis exploration of 72 binary evolution models using COSMIC, varying four key parameters: onset and efficiency of common-envelope evolution, natal kick prescription, and kick treatment during the common envelope phase. BNS formation efficiency and cosmological merger rates are computed under multiple cosmic metallicity-redshift relations.
AI.result: Characteristic metallicity-dependent features were identified (e.g., onset of first-giant-branch skipping at low metallicity, non-monotonic efficiency evolution between Z=10^-3 and 7.5x10^-3). All models predict a bimodal progenitor mass distribution from two formation channels. CE ejection efficiency and natal kicks dominate uncertainty, varying results by orders of magnitude. Different parameter combinations yield similar merger-rate histories, revealing significant degeneracies. Current GW observations only rule out the least efficient models.
AI.conclusion: Breaking parameter degeneracies requires larger BNS merger samples from third-generation gravitational-wave observatories and improved observational constraints on cosmic metallicity evolution, as current data cannot discriminate among most population-synthesis models.

title: Galactic HII regions in LAMOST Medium-Resolution Spectroscopic Survey of Nebulae
summary: Based on LAMOST Medium-Resolution Spectroscopic Survey of Nebulae (MRS-N) data and WISE Galactic HII region catalog, we construct a sample of 280 Galactic HII regions and candidates in the Outer Galaxy (80$^{\circ}$ $\lesssim$ l $\lesssim$ 220$^{\circ}$). Using MRS-N optical spectra, we measure four emission lines (H$α$, [NII]$λ$6584, [SII]$λλ$6717,6731) and use line-ratios to spectroscopically confirm 255 HII regions, including 90 previously "Known" HII regions and 165 newly classified ones. We measure their $T_{\rm e}$, $n_{\rm e}$ and oxygen abundance, and determine distances via associated OB stars and the kinematic method. The sample spans $R_{\rm gal}$ from 8.16 to 15.36 kpc, enabling investigation of radial gradients in physical properties. We find [NII]/H$α$ and [SII]/H$α$ decrease with increasing $R_{\rm gal}$, while [SII]/[NII] remains nearly flat; these trends are quite different from diffuse ionized gas (DIG). We derive the $T_{\rm e}$ gradient of 344.530 $\pm$ 78.083 K kpc$^{-1}$, and the $\log n_{\rm e}$ gradient of -0.143 $\pm$ 0.041 cm$^{-3}$ kpc$^{-1}$. Oxygen abundance shows a steep slope of -0.044 $\pm$ 0.010 dex kpc$^{-1}$ in the inner disk and a shallow slope of -0.016 $\pm$ 0.005 dex kpc$^{-1}$ in the outer disk, with a global slope of -0.014 $\pm$ 0.005 dex kpc$^{-1}$. We also examine the two-dimensional distributions of $T_{\rm e}$, $n_{\rm e}$, and oxygen abundance, and find the gradients vary with azimuth. There is no obvious difference between spiral arm and interarm regions, and no trend appears along individual arms. From [NII]/H$α$-[SII]$λ$6717/H$α$ diagram, HII regions have a S$^+$/S ratio (0.32), lower than DIG (0.43); however, heavy overlap prevents clear separation from this diagram alone.

AI.tldr: A sample of 280 HII regions and candidates in the Outer Galaxy (80°≤l≤220°) is constructed from LAMOST MRS-N and WISE data. Using optical spectra, 255 are spectroscopically confirmed as HII regions. The paper measures Te, ne, and oxygen abundances, determines distances, and investigates radial gradients: Te gradient of 344.5 K/kpc, log ne gradient of -0.143 cm⁻³/kpc, and a steep-to-shallow broken oxygen abundance gradient. Azimuthal variations in gradients are found, but no spiral arm vs interarm differences. HII regions have lower S+/S ratio than DIG but with heavy overlap.
AI.motivation: To build a comprehensive sample of Galactic HII regions in the Outer Galaxy and derive their physical properties (Te, ne, oxygen abundance) and radial gradients, which are key for understanding chemical evolution and the structure of the Milky Way.
AI.method: Construct a sample of 280 HII regions/candidates from LAMOST MRS-N spectra and WISE Galactic HII region catalog. Measure four optical emission lines (Hα, [NII]λ6584, [SII]λλ6717,6731) and use line ratios for spectral classification. Derive Te, ne, and oxygen abundance. Determine distances via associated OB stars and kinematic method. Analyze radial gradients and 2D distributions.
AI.result: 255 HII regions confirmed (90 known, 165 newly classified). Sample spans Rgal 8.16–15.36 kpc. Found [NII]/Hα and [SII]/Hα decrease with Rgal while [SII]/[NII] stays flat, differing from DIG. Te gradient 344.5±78.1 K/kpc; log ne gradient -0.143±0.041 cm⁻³/kpc. Oxygen abundance gradient is steep (-0.044 dex/kpc) in inner disk and shallow (-0.016 dex/kpc) in outer disk, global slope -0.014±0.005 dex/kpc. Gradients vary with azimuth; no arm/interarm difference. S+/S ratio of HII regions (0.32) lower than DIG (0.43) but with heavy overlap.
AI.conclusion: The Outer Galaxy HII regions show distinct radial gradients in physical properties, with a broken (steep-to-shallow) oxygen abundance gradient. Azimuthal variations exist but no spiral arm dependence. The line-ratio diagnostics differ from DIG, but a single diagnostic diagram cannot fully separate them due to heavy overlap.

title: Radio Follow-Up of Einstein Probe Fast X-Ray Transients
summary: Fast X-ray transients (FXTs) are brief, luminous bursts of soft X-ray emission whose physical origins remain uncertain. The Einstein Probe (EP) mission has recently enabled prompt discovery of these events, providing opportunities for rapid multi-wavelength follow-up. We present a coordinated radio observing campaign targeting 20 FXTs detected by the EP in 2024. The core consists of 59 epochs with the Allen Telescope Array (ATA), sampling post-burst timescales from $\sim$1 to $\sim$65 days and reaching typical $3σ$ sensitivities of 0.6--1.5\,mJy across 1--8\,GHz. Two FXTs---EP240315a and EP241021a---have radio counterparts. For EP241021a, AMI-LA monitoring at 15.5\,GHz reveals a light curve peaking at $\sim$30 days with $F_ν\approx1.0$\,mJy; equipartition analysis implies a Newtonian equipartition energy of $\sim3\times10^{49}$\,erg and a mildly relativistic on-axis solution with $Γ_{\rm on}\approx1.3$. Multi-frequency modelling of EP240315a, combining new VLA measurements with published MeerKAT, ATCA, and eMERLIN data, indicates highly relativistic early emission ($Γ\gtrsim3$) that decelerates with time, consistent with jetted outflow. The detections and ATA non-detections span luminosities overlapping the brightest GRB and relativistic tidal disruption event (TDE) afterglows, suggesting FXTs comprise a heterogeneous population including both relativistic and non-relativistic explosions. Under a GRB-like redshift prior, our $3σ$ ATA limits correspond to observer-frame specific-luminosity thresholds of $\sim10^{32}$--$10^{33}\,\mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ Hz^{-1}}$; for nearby events ($z\lesssim0.2$), $L_ν\lesssim10^{30\text{--}31}\,\mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}\ Hz^{-1}}$. Planned ATA upgrades and next-generation arrays (SKA, DSA, ngVLA) will enable sensitive, population-level radio studies of the FXT radio sky.

AI.tldr: A coordinated radio campaign with the Allen Telescope Array targeted 20 Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) detected by the Einstein Probe in 2024, spanning ~1-65 days post-burst at 1-8 GHz. Two FXTs (EP240315a and EP241021a) had radio counterparts. EP241021a showed a light curve peaking at ~30 days with mildly relativistic emission (Γ~1.3), while EP240315a exhibited highly relativistic, decelerating jetted emission (Γ≳3). The results indicate FXTs are a heterogeneous population spanning both relativistic and non-relativistic explosions, overlapping GRB and TDE afterglow luminosities.
AI.motivation: FXTs are brief, luminous soft X-ray bursts of uncertain physical origin. The Einstein Probe's prompt discovery capabilities enable rapid multi-wavelength follow-up, motivating a systematic radio study to characterize the nature of these transients.
AI.method: A coordinated radio observing campaign with 59 epochs from the Allen Telescope Array (1-8 GHz, 3σ sensitivities of 0.6-1.5 mJy) targeting 20 FXTs discovered by the Einstein Probe in 2024, supplemented by AMI-LA 15.5 GHz monitoring, VLA, MeerKAT, ATCA, and eMERLIN observations, with equipartition and multi-frequency modelling.
AI.result: Two radio counterparts found: EP241021a (peaking at ~30 days, F_ν≈1.0 mJy, equipartition energy ~3×10^49 erg, Γ_on≈1.3) and EP240315a (highly relativistic, Γ≳3, decelerating jetted outflow). ATA limits imply luminosity thresholds of ~10^32-10^33 erg/s/Hz (GRB-like prior) and ~10^30-31 erg/s/Hz for nearby events at z≲0.2.
AI.conclusion: FXTs comprise a heterogeneous population including both relativistic and non-relativistic explosions, with radio luminosities overlapping the brightest GRB and relativistic TDE afterglows. Upcoming facilities (SKA, DSA, ngVLA) and ATA upgrades will enable population-level radio studies of FXTs.

title: The X-ray-Weak Tail of the Quasar Population: Physical Properties and Redshift Evolution of Variability-Selected AGN in eFEDS
summary: (abridged) Aims: To characterize variability-selected AGN candidates within the eROSITA Final Equatorial-Depth Survey (eFEDS), leveraging the synergy between optical variability and deep X-ray observations by SRG (Spectrum Roentgen Gamma)/eROSITA, to compare the physical properties of AGN populations selected through complementary methods. Methods: We used a sample of AGN candidates selected via optical variability by Arévalo et al. and cross-match it to the X-ray selected eFEDS AGN sample. Spectroscopic characterizations are obtained for the matched samples from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument public data products. Results: We find a high classification purity with 98% candidates confirmed as broad-line AGN/QSOs. We identify a significant population (25%) that lack X-ray counterparts (X-U) in the eFEDS survey. We find that the X-D and X-U samples exhibit distinct physical properties and redshift distributions. The X-U sample peaks at $z = 2$ while the X-D sample at $z =1$, with nearly half of the variability-selected AGN at $z > 2.5$ remaining undetected in X-rays. This missing fraction can be attributed to K-correction effects and SED evolution with luminosity, mainly resulting in high accretion rate objects falling out of the X-D sample at higher redshifts. X-ray variability accounts for a part of the missing fraction but its dependence with redshift is less clear. Ensemble spectral analysis reveals that X-D sources have steeper optical continua and stronger broad emission lines than their X-U counterparts, while the forbidden and semi-forbidden lines have equal EWs in both samples. Finally, broad absorption line (BAL) features are found almost exclusively in the X-U population. This "missing" X-ray population must be accounted for when extrapolating X-ray-selected AGN to the broader Type I population and could impact cosmic estimates of massive black hole growth.

AI.tldr: This study characterizes variability-selected AGN candidates in the eROSITA Final Equatorial-Depth Survey (eFEDS), finding 98% are confirmed broad-line AGN/QSOs. A significant 25% lack X-ray counterparts, peaking at z=2 versus z=1 for X-ray-detected sources. The missing X-ray population is attributed to K-correction, SED evolution with luminosity (high accretion rate objects), and partially to X-ray variability. X-ray-detected sources show steeper optical continua and stronger broad emission lines, while BAL features appear almost exclusively in the X-ray-undetected population, with implications for cosmic estimates of massive black hole growth.
AI.motivation: To leverage the synergy between optical variability selection and deep X-ray observations to characterize AGN populations selected through complementary methods, understand why a significant fraction of variability-selected AGN are missing in X-ray surveys, and assess implications for extrapolating X-ray-selected AGN to the broader Type I population.
AI.method: Cross-matched optical variability-selected AGN candidates (from Arévalo et al.) with the X-ray selected eFEDS AGN sample from SRG/eROSITA. Obtained spectroscopic classifications from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) public data products. Compared physical properties, redshift distributions, and performed ensemble spectral analysis of the matched samples.
AI.result: Found 98% classification purity (broad-line AGN/QSOs). Identified 25% of variability-selected AGN lacking X-ray counterparts (X-U). X-D sample peaks at z=1 while X-U peaks at z=2, with nearly half of z>2.5 AGN undetected in X-rays. Missing fraction attributed mainly to K-correction and SED evolution with luminosity (high accretion rate objects drop out at high z), with X-ray variability a partial contributor. X-D sources have steeper optical continua and stronger broad lines; forbidden and semi-forbidden lines show equal EWs. BAL features found almost exclusively in X-U population.
AI.conclusion: The variability-selected AGN population contains a significant X-ray-undetected component that must be accounted for when extrapolating X-ray-selected AGN samples to the broader Type I AGN population. This missing population could bias cosmic estimates of massive black hole growth and accretion history.

title: On the triple nature of the PSR J0435+3233 system
summary: Context. The recent pulsar timing ephemeris of PSR J0435+3233 indicates that this millisecond pulsar (MSP) has a spin-down rate that is much higher than observed in other MSPs and challenges our understanding of the formation and evolution of MSPs. Aims. We propose that this system is a hierarchical triple, and that the high spin-down rate is caused by varying acceleration due to a tertiary in a wide orbit. Methods. We use pulsar timing methods with radio and gamma-ray observations of PSR J0435+3233 to determine the system properties. Results. We find that a hierarchical triple timing model describes the timing observations of PSR J0435+3233 and that this results in the detection of gamma-ray pulsations back to the beginning of the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) data in 2008. The intrinsic spin-down rate remains uncertain as it correlates with the parameters of the outer orbit, but large spin-down rates are excluded and the intrinsic rate is at least two orders of magnitude lower than the observed rate, in line with other Galactic MSPs. We identify a star located 11 mas from the pulsar position as the optical counterpart to the tertiary companion. From the 1.5-2.5 kpc distance and colours, we infer that the tertiary is a 1.2 solar mass F-type main-sequence star. Along with the pulsar binary, it orbits the common centre of mass with an eccentric (e ~ 0.6), wide (~ 70 yr) orbit that is likely seen at a low orbital inclination. Conclusions. We conclude that PSR J0435+3233 is a hierarchical triple system. We discuss the motivation and prospects for the continued study of this system. Spectral measurements of the outer star in addition to continued astrometric measurements will yield mass ratio and inclination estimates, while continued pulsar timing may yield a tighter constraint on violations of the Strong Equivalence Principle than are currently obtained from PSR J0337+1715.

AI.tldr: PSR J0435+3233, an MSP with an anomalously high observed spin-down rate, is identified as a hierarchical triple system. A wide, eccentric (~70 yr) outer orbit with a 1.2 solar mass F-type main-sequence tertiary causes the apparent high spin-down via varying acceleration. Modeling this system reduces the intrinsic spin-down to values consistent with other Galactic MSPs and enables detection of gamma-ray pulsations back to 2008. The system may provide tighter constraints on Strong Equivalence Principle violations than PSR J0337+1715.
AI.motivation: The observed spin-down rate of PSR J0435+3233 is much higher than that of typical MSPs, challenging our understanding of MSP formation and evolution. The authors propose a hierarchical triple explanation to resolve this discrepancy.
AI.method: The authors use pulsar timing techniques applied to radio and gamma-ray (Fermi LAT) observations. They model the system as a hierarchical triple, fit the timing data, identify the optical counterpart via astrometric and photometric measurements, and infer the outer orbit's properties.
AI.result: A hierarchical triple model fits the timing data, enabling gamma-ray pulsation detection from 2008. The intrinsic spin-down is at least two orders of magnitude lower than observed, consistent with other MSPs. A companion star at 11 mas, a 1.2 solar mass F-type main-sequence star at 1.5-2.5 kpc, is identified. The outer orbit is wide (~70 yr) and eccentric (e~0.6) at likely low inclination.
AI.conclusion: PSR J0435+3233 is a hierarchical triple system. Continued study, including spectral, astrometric, and longer pulsar timing observations, may yield tighter constraints on violations of the Strong Equivalence Principle than currently available from PSR J0337+1715.

title: Revealing the Physical Driver of the Baldwin Effect: Gas Density in the Broad-Line Region
comment: Comments: 11 pages, 7 figures, 4 appendix figures. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The Baldwin effect --- the inverse correlation between the equivalent width of emission lines and the continuum luminosity in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) --- has been known for nearly five decades, yet its physical origin remains poorly understood. Using a sample of 41,159 radio quasars constructed from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Low-Frequency Array Two-metre Sky Survey, we investigate the origin and underlying physics of the Baldwin effect of MgII broad emission lines in both radio-quiet (RQ) and radio-loud (RL) quasars. We find that the slope $β$ of the Baldwin effect is positively correlated with the Eddington ratio $λ_{\rm Edd}$ in both populations, and RL quasars exhibit steeper $β$ than their RQ quasars at fixed $λ_{\rm Edd}$. Photoionization simulations reveal that the $β$ is primarily governed by the gas density in the broad-line region (BLR): lower gas densities yield steeper slopes. This density-driven mechanism naturally connects the Baldwin effect to the broader AGN evolutionary context. Specifically, higher $λ_{\rm Edd}$ drive stronger accretion disk winds, leading to denser BLRs and shallower $β$. Our findings indicate that BLR gas density serves as the primary physical driver underlying the "global" Baldwin effect, offering a physically grounded framework for interpreting AGN accretion states and their coupled evolution with host galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using 41,159 radio quasars from SDSS and LoTSS, this study reveals that the Baldwin effect slope (β) in MgII emission lines is positively correlated with Eddington ratio (λ_Edd) in both radio-quiet and radio-loud quasars. Photoionization simulations show gas density in the broad-line region is the primary physical driver: lower densities yield steeper β slopes. This density-driven mechanism links the Baldwin effect to AGN evolution through accretion disk winds.
AI.motivation: The Baldwin effect has been known for nearly five decades, but its physical origin remains poorly understood. This study aims to uncover the underlying physics driving this inverse correlation between emission-line equivalent width and continuum luminosity in AGNs.
AI.method: The authors constructed a sample of 41,159 radio quasars from Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and Low-Frequency Array Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) data. They investigated the MgII broad emission line Baldwin effect separately in radio-quiet (RQ) and radio-loud (RL) quasars, and performed photoionization simulations to identify the governing physical parameter.
AI.result: The Baldwin effect slope β is positively correlated with the Eddington ratio λ_Edd in both RQ and RL quasars. RL quasars show steeper β than RQ quasars at fixed λ_Edd. Photoionization simulations demonstrate that β is primarily governed by the gas density in the broad-line region, with lower gas densities producing steeper slopes.
AI.conclusion: Broad-line region gas density is the primary physical driver of the "global" Baldwin effect. Higher Eddington ratios drive stronger accretion disk winds, producing denser BLRs and shallower β slopes. This provides a physically grounded framework connecting the Baldwin effect to AGN accretion states and host galaxy co-evolution.

title: JWST Spectra Indicate a Large Mass of Postshock Dust Formed by SN 2010jl
summary: We present new JWST mid-IR spectra and ground-based optical spectra of the lingering source at the position of SN 2010jl, which was a relatively nearby superluminous Type IIn supernova having strong interaction with circumstellar material (CSM). Early-time data showed evidence of dust, interpreted as either pre-existing CSM dust, or as newly formed dust in the SN ejecta and post-shock region. At 13 yr post explosion, JWST reveals a strong MIR excess from warm dust, with broad features at 10-15 $μ$m. Our analysis reveals a minimum dust mass of $>$0.11 $M_{\odot}$, and a more likely value of 0.2 $M_{\odot}$ or more because the dust is optically thick. This is among the largest masses of SN-produced dust yet measured without far-IR/submm data, and greatly exceeds SN 2010jl's dust mass inferred around 2-3 yr post-explosion. Ground-based optical spectra confirm the presence of a young massive cluster at the SN position, and confirm that blueshifted line profiles persisting until the latest epochs arise from dust formed in the post-shock region. The warmest dust emitting in the MIR is likely to be the same post-shock dust causing the blueshift. The JWST spectrum also reveals silicate absorption, which may arise from cool SN ejecta dust along the line of sight to the receding shock. The large mass of post-shock dust in SN 2010jl suggests that strong CSM interaction promotes efficient dust production, where the new post-shock dust will survive. If strongly interacting SNe are common in the early Universe, this may contribute significantly to dust seen in infant galaxies.

AI.tldr: JWST mid-IR and optical observations of the lingering source at the position of SN 2010jl, 13 years post-explosion, reveal a large mass of warm dust (>0.11 M_sun, likely ~0.2 M_sun or more) with broad 10-15 micron features, confirming that strongly interacting Type IIn SNe can efficiently produce massive amounts of post-shock dust that may contribute significantly to dust in infant galaxies.
AI.motivation: To determine whether dust in SN 2010jl is pre-existing CSM dust or newly formed dust in the SN ejecta/post-shock region, and to measure the total dust mass produced by a strongly interacting superluminous Type IIn supernova at late times.
AI.method: Combined JWST mid-infrared spectroscopy with ground-based optical spectroscopy of the SN 2010jl location at 13 years post-explosion, analyzing the MIR spectral energy distribution, broad features at 10-15 microns, silicate absorption, and blueshifted line profiles to derive dust mass and location.
AI.result: The analysis yields a minimum dust mass of >0.11 M_sun, with a more likely value of 0.2 M_sun or more (dust being optically thick). This is among the largest SN-produced dust masses measured without far-IR/submm data, greatly exceeding earlier estimates at 2-3 years. The warmest MIR-emitting dust is identified as post-shock dust causing the blueshifted line profiles, and silicate absorption suggests cool SN ejecta dust along the line of sight.
AI.conclusion: Strong CSM interaction promotes efficient and massive dust production in SN 2010jl, where the newly formed post-shock dust survives. If such strongly interacting SNe are common in the early Universe, they may contribute significantly to the dust observed in infant galaxies.

title: The eROSITA X-ray luminosity function of active galactic nuclei
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures. Catalogue including redshift information is released via the eROSITA web pages and CDS upon the journal's article acceptance
summary: The X-ray luminosity function (XLF) of active galactic nuclei (AGN) provides an observational probe of the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) across cosmic time. With its large survey grasp, Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA samples the luminosity--redshift plane with a depth--area balance complementary to pencil-beam surveys, providing the volume needed to detect rare luminous AGN, previously limited by small-number statistics. We measure the soft XLF, leveraging an eROSITA sample spanning approximately eight orders of magnitude in luminosity out to $z\simeq6$. This enables us to study luminosity-dependent evolution with improved constraints, and to infer both the SMBH accretion history and optical/UV missed AGN population. We introduce a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterisation in which all XLF model parameters are allowed to evolve continuously with redshift. We find lower space densities for moderately and very luminous AGN at low redshift, while the abundance is higher than previously found at the highest redshifts. Comparisons to optical/UV quasar LFs converted to rest-frame $2\!-\!10\,\mathrm{keV}$ show that the UV-missed fraction decreases with luminosity, and, in the most luminous bin, increases with redshift. Integrating the XLF yields a black-hole accretion-rate density peaking at $z \simeq 1.5$, with the corresponding cumulative black-hole mass density indicating $\sim80^{+11}_{-23}\%$ obscured growth relative to locally-inferred BH mass estimates derived from scaling relations and missed by the soft X-ray selection of our sample. With this work, we release the eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue, including counterparts and their redshift information. We then discuss how these results can inform future spectroscopic, photometric, and X-ray survey strategies aimed at improving AGN demographic constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the soft X-ray luminosity function of AGN using the SRG/eROSITA sample spanning ~8 orders of magnitude in luminosity out to z≈6. The authors introduce a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterisation, find lower space densities of luminous AGN at low redshift but higher abundances at high redshift, estimate ~80% obscured SMBH growth relative to local estimates, and release the eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue.
AI.motivation: To overcome small-number statistics that previously limited constraints on rare luminous AGN, and to provide improved measurements of luminosity-dependent evolution, SMBH accretion history, and the optically/UV-missed AGN population using the large survey grasp of eROSITA.
AI.method: Uses an eROSITA soft X-ray AGN sample spanning ~eight orders of magnitude in luminosity out to z≃6. Introduces a new redshift-dependent smoothly broken power-law parameterisation of the XLF in which all model parameters evolve continuously with redshift. Compares to optical/UV quasar LFs converted to rest-frame 2-10 keV, integrates the XLF to derive accretion-rate density, and estimates obscured growth fraction.
AI.result: Finds lower space densities of moderately and very luminous AGN at low redshift but higher abundances at high redshift than previously reported. The UV-missed fraction decreases with luminosity and increases with redshift in the most luminous bin. The black-hole accretion-rate density peaks at z≃1.5, with cumulative black-hole mass density indicating ~80% obscured growth missed by soft X-ray selection.
AI.conclusion: The eROSITA DR2 AGN catalogue is released with counterparts and redshifts. Results inform future spectroscopic, photometric, and X-ray survey strategies for improving AGN demographic constraints, particularly regarding the substantial obscured growth fraction.

title: Depolarization Induced by Rapid Polarization Angle Swings: A Common Feature of Pulsars and Fast Radio Bursts?
summary: The polarization angle (PA) of pulsars and fast radio bursts (FRBs) provides a useful diagnostic of the magnetic fields in their emission regions and is therefore crucial for understanding their radiation and origins. Within a general geometric framework for polarized emission from a rotating neutron star, we suggest a possible anti-correlation between the degree of linear polarization $Π_\text{L}$ and $d\text{PA}/dt$, the time derivative of the PA, as a common feature of pulsars and FRBs. The depolarization arises from the incoherent superposition of radiation with different polarization directions within the observable part of the emission region, and is detectable only when the PA swing is steep enough. We test this conjecture using a sample of radio pulsars and find possible evidence for the expected anti-correlation in a subset of pulsars. Whether this relation holds in FRBs remains uncertain due to limited observational data. Identification of this feature would not only provide insights into the rotating magnetospheric origin of FRBs, but also place constraints on the spin periods and geometric parameters of the neutron stars that power these mysterious bursts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an anti-correlation between the degree of linear polarization (Π_L) and the time derivative of polarization angle (dPA/dt) in pulsars and fast radio bursts (FRBs), arising from incoherent superposition of differently polarized radiation within the emission region. The prediction is tested against a sample of radio pulsars, showing possible evidence in a subset, while FRB confirmation remains pending due to limited data.
AI.motivation: Polarization angle serves as a key diagnostic for magnetic fields in the emission regions of pulsars and FRBs, and understanding their polarization properties is crucial for determining the radiation mechanisms and origins of these sources. The authors aim to identify a common geometric feature that can help establish whether FRBs share a rotating magnetospheric origin with pulsars.
AI.method: The authors develop a general geometric framework for polarized emission from a rotating neutron star, showing that depolarization results from the incoherent superposition of radiation with different polarization directions within the observable part of the emission region, detectable only when the PA swing is sufficiently steep. They then test the predicted anti-correlation observationally using a sample of radio pulsars.
AI.result: They find possible evidence for the expected anti-correlation between Π_L and dPA/dt in a subset of radio pulsars. The applicability of this relation to FRBs remains uncertain due to limited observational data.
AI.conclusion: Identifying this anti-correlation feature would provide insights into the rotating magnetospheric origin of FRBs and place constraints on the spin periods and geometric parameters of their underlying neutron stars.

title: Invariant manifolds in barred galaxy simulations. III. Self-regulated weakening of strong spiral arms
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in A&A on 30/07/2026
summary: We investigated the origin of the weakening of strong spiral arms in barred galaxies, seeking the physical mechanism responsible for the decline in the fraction of manifold-trapped particles over time. We reconstructed the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body simulation of a barred galaxy using AGAMA, computed the Lagrangian points, and quantified how their spiral-induced angular displacement affects the geometry of the invariant manifolds and the associated orbital flows. We find that sufficiently strong, self-gravitating spiral arms significantly reshape the gravitational potential of a barred galaxy, displacing the equilibrium points up to 20-50° from the bar major axis, where they are expected to lie in the standard invariant-manifold framework. This shift alters the configuration of the manifold branches and disrupts the coherent stellar flows that sustain the spiral structure. As the spiral weakens, the equilibrium points gradually return to their standard configuration, restoring the conditions for manifold-driven spiral arm formation on a timescale of ~200 Gyr. We show for the first time that invariant manifolds and the spiral structures they generate are coupled through a self-regulating feedback mechanism, allowing the spiral pattern to recur over time. Our results therefore indicate that, although barred galaxies may sustain spiral activity over long timescales, individual episodes of strong spiral arms are intrinsically transient.

AI.tldr: Using N-body simulations of barred galaxies and AGAMA potential reconstruction, the authors show that strong self-gravitating spiral arms displace the Lagrangian points 20-50° from the bar major axis, disrupting invariant manifolds and coherent stellar flows. As spirals weaken, equilibrium points return to standard configurations, restoring manifold-driven spiral formation on ~200 Gyr timescales, revealing a self-regulating feedback between manifolds and spiral arms.
AI.motivation: To uncover the physical mechanism behind the observed decline in manifold-trapped particle fractions over time in barred galaxies, i.e., to explain why strong spiral arms in barred galaxies weaken.
AI.method: Reconstruct the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body barred-galaxy simulation using AGAMA, compute the Lagrangian points, and quantify how spiral-induced angular displacement of equilibrium points affects the geometry of invariant manifolds and associated orbital flows.
AI.result: Strong self-gravitating spirals displace the Lagrangian points by 20-50° from the bar major axis, disrupting manifold branches and coherent stellar flows. When spirals weaken, equilibrium points return to standard positions, restoring manifold-driven spiral formation on a ~200 Gyr timescale. This constitutes a novel self-regulating feedback loop between manifolds and spirals.
AI.conclusion: Invariant manifolds and spiral structures are coupled via a self-regulating feedback that allows spiral recurrence over long timescales, yet individual strong-spiral episodes are intrinsically transient in barred galaxies.

title: An extra hard spectral component peaking at sub-GeV in the prompt emission of GRB 260226A
summary: The prompt emission spectra of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) have long been empirically described by the Band function over the keV--MeV range, whereas several \textit{Fermi}/LAT-detected GRBs show evidence for an extra hard component at higher energies. Here we present a joint GBM--LAT study of GRB~260226A, a rare LAT seeded onboard trigger GRB, and find that an extra sub-GeV component is present. In the time-resolved analysis, we find that a cutoff power-law model fits the spectral data of the extra component better than other models at earlier times, while at later times, the broken power-law model is preferred (or at least equally good). Interpreting the early cutoff as the $γγ$ absorption implies that the Lorentz factor at early time is lower and increases with time. The low ratio between the peak energy of the extra component and that of the Band component is difficult to explain with a one-zone synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) scenario. Two-zone emission models, such as external inverse Compton scattering of the photosphere emission by relativistic electrons accelerated in internal shocks, could provide a possible explanation.

AI.tldr: A joint GBM-LAT spectral analysis of GRB 260226A reveals an extra sub-GeV component beyond the standard Band function. The extra component is best described by a cutoff power-law at early times (interpreted as gamma-gamma absorption, implying a lower and increasing Lorentz factor) and a broken power-law at later times. The observed peak-energy ratio disfavors one-zone SSC models, while two-zone external inverse Compton scenarios offer a plausible explanation.
AI.motivation: The prompt emission spectra of GRBs are traditionally modeled with the Band function in the keV-MeV band, but several Fermi/LAT-detected GRBs show an additional hard component at higher energies. This paper aims to study GRB 260226A, a rare LAT seeded onboard trigger GRB, to characterize this extra sub-GeV component and understand its physical origin.
AI.method: Joint GBM-LAT time-resolved spectral analysis of GRB 260226A was performed. Spectral fitting was used to compare a cutoff power-law model against other models at early times, and a broken power-law model at later times, for the extra sub-GeV component. Interpretations were made regarding gamma-gamma absorption effects on the early cutoff and the ratio of peak energies to test one-zone SSC versus two-zone emission scenarios.
AI.result: An extra sub-GeV component is present in GRB 260226A. The cutoff power-law model fits best at early times while the broken power-law model is preferred (or equally good) at later times. The early cutoff is consistent with gamma-gamma absorption, implying a lower Lorentz factor that increases with time. The low peak-energy ratio relative to the Band component is difficult to explain with one-zone SSC; two-zone models such as external inverse Compton scattering of photospheric emission by internal-shock-accelerated electrons provide a plausible alternative.
AI.conclusion: GRB 260226A exhibits an extra high-energy component that evolves in spectral shape from a cutoff power-law to a broken power-law over time. The results favor a two-zone emission scenario over one-zone SSC, and suggest a time-evolving Lorentz factor in the emitting region.

title: A search for HI absorption in distant star-forming galaxies with ASKAP-FLASH - II. Direct observations and stacking of 21 cm line
