comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present results of a search for associated and intervening HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies at 0.4 < $z$ < 1.0, using ASKAP's FLASH HI 21 cm absorption survey. We report the detection of a new HI 21 cm absorption line in radio galaxy NVSS J214954-004657 at $z_{\mathrm{HI}}$ = 0.863. Additionally, we present results of HI 21 cm stacking for associated and intervening star-forming and radio galaxy catalogues. For the first time at these redshifts, we report tentative detections of stacked HI 21 cm absorption for associated galaxies when stacked in order of descending radio source brightness, and show that these tentative detections become buried as optical depth increases as progressively weaker sources are co-added into the stack. No stacked signal is detected when co-adding intervening galaxy spectra. We speculate that the ability to detect a stacked HI 21 cm detection is dependent on the background source optical depth limits, as well as source covering factors. Covering factor has a greater impact when stacking intervening systems, and can be considered to effectively weaken the observed flux density of a radio source. We find no significant difference in detection rate for associated HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies versus the general radio-source population at the same redshift. Although detection rates are low, from a meta-analysis of HI 21 cm surveys we find that 1 detection is expected given the survey parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first search for HI 21 cm absorption in associated and intervening star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies at 0.4 < z < 1.0 using ASKAP's FLASH survey. A new HI 21 cm absorption line was detected in radio galaxy NVSS J214954-004657 at z = 0.863, and tentative stacked HI 21 cm detections are reported for associated galaxies when stacked by descending radio brightness. These stacked detections become buried as weaker sources are added, no stacked signal is found for intervening galaxies, and no significant difference in detection rates between star-forming and general radio-source populations is found.
AI.motivation: To search for HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies and radio galaxies at intermediate redshifts (0.4 < z < 1.0), a regime where few such measurements exist. The study aims to understand HI gas content and its relation to star formation and radio activity in galaxies, using both individual detections and stacking analyses from a large-survey dataset.
AI.method: The authors used ASKAP's FLASH HI 21 cm absorption survey to search for both associated and intervening HI absorption toward star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies at 0.4 < z < 1.0. They performed individual line searches and applied HI 21 cm stacking techniques on galaxy catalogues, including stacking in order of descending radio source brightness to investigate detectability. A meta-analysis of HI 21 cm surveys was also conducted to compare expected vs. actual detection rates.
AI.result: A new HI 21 cm absorption line was detected in radio galaxy NVSS J214954-004657 at z_HI = 0.863. Tentative stacked detections of associated HI 21 cm absorption were found for the first time at these redshifts when stacking by descending radio source brightness, but these signals become buried as weaker sources are co-added. No stacked signal was detected for intervening galaxies. No significant difference in associated detection rates was found between star-forming and general radio-source populations, and one detection is expected from meta-analysis given the survey parameters.
AI.conclusion: The detectability of stacked HI 21 cm absorption depends on background source optical depth limits and source covering factors. Covering factor has a greater impact on intervening systems, effectively weakening the observed radio flux density. The findings suggest that HI 21 cm absorption detection rates for associated star-forming galaxies are comparable to the general radio-source population at the same redshift, and low detection rates are consistent with survey expectations.

title: On the Blueprint of Active Galaxies Producing Neutrinos
summary: Based on the observation of the active galaxies NGC 1068 and TXS 0506+056, and on additional evidence for the sources NGC 4151, CGCG 420-015, NGC 7469, and the Circinus Galaxy emerging from IceCube data, we make the case for the production of high-energy neutrinos within a few gravitational radii of supermassive black holes surrounded by a dense plasma radiating X-rays. X-rays represents the target for the production of neutrinos by protons accelerated near the black hole; they also absorb the gamma rays from the decay of neutral pions produced in the same interactions. Neutrinos with energies of tens of TeV and above originate in photoproduction interactions with X-rays of $0.1 \sim 1$\,keV energy on the $Δ$ resonance, $p + γ\rightarrow Δ\rightarrow n + π^+$. Our analysis of the multimessenger data points to gamma-ray-obscured sources with a characteristic neutrino flux linearly proportional to the X-ray flux originating within $\sim 10$ gravitational radii of the black holes, with lower values preferred. We speculate on such sources producing the diffuse flux of neutrinos and cosmic rays of extragalactic origin.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that high-energy neutrinos (tens of TeV and above) are produced within a few gravitational radii of supermassive black holes in gamma-ray-obscured active galactic nuclei, where protons accelerated near the black hole interact with 0.1-1 keV X-rays via the Δ resonance (p+γ→Δ→n+π+). Analysis of multimessenger data from NGC 1068, TXS 0506+056, and other IceCube sources suggests a neutrino flux linearly proportional to the X-ray flux originating within ~10 gravitational radii, and speculates these sources contribute to the diffuse extragalactic neutrino and cosmic-ray flux.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos detected by IceCube, particularly the neutral-pion production in gamma-ray-obscured environments near supermassive black holes, using X-rays as targets for photoproduction while also absorbing the accompanying gamma rays.
AI.method: Multimessenger analysis combining IceCube neutrino observations of active galaxies (NGC 1068, TXS 0506+056, NGC 4151, CGCG 420-015, NGC 7469, Circinus Galaxy) with X-ray data, examining photoproduction interactions on the Δ resonance with 0.1-1 keV X-rays.
AI.result: The data support gamma-ray-obscured sources with a neutrino flux that scales linearly with X-ray flux, originating within ~10 gravitational radii of supermassive black holes, with smaller radii preferred.
AI.conclusion: These gamma-ray-obscured sources near supermassive black holes are likely contributors to the diffuse flux of extragalactic neutrinos and cosmic rays, establishing X-ray emission as a key tracer for neutrino production.

title: Angular Momentum Evolution from Core to Disk Scales in the Early Phase of Star Formation: Constraints from HH 212, HH 211, and B335
summary: I investigate the angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation using three protostellar systems: HH 212, HH 211, and B335. Observations show that the specific angular momentum follows a power-law dependence at core scales and transitions to an approximately constant value at smaller radii, indicating dynamical collapse in the inner envelope. I model this behavior using the inside-out collapse solution of Shu (1977) and its rotating extension, the Terebey-Shu-Cassen model, including modest magnetic effects through a flattened, magnetized core. I find that the observed angular momentum profiles in all three sources are broadly consistent with an inside-out collapse scenario with approximate conservation of specific angular momentum in the collapsing region. The inferred collapse ages and mass infall rates yield total masses accreted onto the center that are broadly consistent with the central masses derived from kinematics, allowing for a fraction of the material to be ejected by jets and winds. The predicted midplane densities at typical radii, including the effect of magnetic flattening, are also consistent with observational estimates. The three systems exhibit a similar pattern of angular momentum evolution despite large differences in the magnitude of their specific angular momentum. In particular, the small disk in B335 can be naturally explained by its lower initial specific angular momentum, although alternative explanations, such as magnetic braking or different initial conditions, cannot be excluded. These results suggest that inside-out collapse, with modest magnetic modification, provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in early star formation across three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, B335), finding that observed profiles are consistent with inside-out collapse (Shu 1977; Terebey-Shu-Cassen) with modest magnetic effects, and that differences in disk sizes stem primarily from differing initial specific angular momentum.
AI.motivation: To understand how angular momentum evolves from molecular cloud core scales down to disk scales during early star formation, and to test whether the standard inside-out collapse paradigm (with modest magnetic modification) can explain the observed angular momentum profiles in real protostellar systems.
AI.method: The author compares observed specific angular momentum profiles of three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, B335) against theoretical models: the inside-out collapse solution of Shu (1977) and its rotating extension, the Terebey-Shu-Cassen model, with modest magnetic effects incorporated via a flattened, magnetized core. Collapse ages and mass infall rates are inferred and compared with kinematically derived central masses and observational density estimates.
AI.result: All three sources show angular momentum profiles broadly consistent with inside-out collapse with approximate specific angular momentum conservation in the collapsing region. Inferred collapse ages and infall rates yield accreted masses consistent with kinematically derived central masses (accounting for jet/wind ejection). Predicted midplane densities including magnetic flattening match observations. Despite large differences in specific angular momentum magnitude, all three exhibit similar evolution patterns, with B335's small disk naturally explained by its lower initial specific angular momentum.
AI.conclusion: Inside-out collapse with modest magnetic modification provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in early star formation, though alternative explanations (magnetic braking, different initial conditions) for the small B335 disk cannot be excluded.

title: Distinct Jet Properties in the X-Ray-Obscured State of GRS 1915+105
comment: This is a revised manuscript submitted to ApJ
summary: GRS 1915+105 has remained in an X-ray-obscured state since its transition from a long-lasting unobscured state in 2019. We report on 6.7-GHz East Asia VLBI Network observations of GRS 1915+105 obtained during strong radio flares detected at 2.3--11.2 GHz with the RATAN-600 radio telescope in 2025. Our images reveal two contrasting jet morphologies. The first epoch, associated with a flare evolving from an optically thick to an optically thin spectrum, shows a bright radio core accompanied by an extended jet structure. By contrast, the second epoch, observed near the peak of another flare displaying optically thin emission at lower frequencies, is dominated by two bright, symmetric, well-separated jet blobs and shows no detectable radio core. If these jets exhibited the apparent superluminal motions commonly observed prior to 2019, measurable angular shifts would be expected over the five-hour observations. However, no significant jet motion is detected. Combined with our derived jet speed of $βΓ\lesssim 0.40$, these results suggest that the jets launched during the current obscured state are slower than the relativistic jets ($βΓ\gtrsim 1$) observed earlier during the unobscured state. Together with the recently reported large variations in jet orientation, our findings in GRS 1915+105 provide robust support for the emerging paradigm that X-ray binary jets launched in obscured and unobscured states likely exhibit distinct propagation properties.

AI.tldr: This paper reports on 6.7-GHz East Asia VLBI Network observations of the microquasar GRS 1915+105 during strong radio flares in 2025, revealing two contrasting jet morphologies. No significant jet motion is detected, and the derived jet speed (βΓ≲0.40) suggests that jets launched during the current X-ray-obscured state are slower than the relativistic jets (βΓ≳1) observed during the earlier unobscured state, supporting the paradigm that jets in obscured and unobscured states exhibit distinct propagation properties.
AI.motivation: To investigate the jet properties of GRS 1915+105 during its current X-ray-obscured state (since 2019), and to test whether jets launched in different accretion states exhibit different propagation characteristics.
AI.method: The authors used 6.7-GHz East Asia VLBI Network (EAVN) observations of GRS 1915+105 during strong radio flares detected at 2.3–11.2 GHz with RATAN-600, producing high-resolution images to analyze jet morphology, angular shifts, and jet speed constraints.
AI.result: Two epochs revealed contrasting jet morphologies: the first showed a bright core with extended jet structure during an optically thick-to-thin transition, while the second showed two bright, symmetric, well-separated jet blobs with no detectable core near a flare peak with optically thin emission. No significant jet motion was detected over five-hour observations, and the derived jet speed upper limit is βΓ≲0.40, slower than the relativistic jets (βΓ≳1) seen earlier.
AI.conclusion: The jets launched during the obscured state of GRS 1915+105 appear slower than those from the unobscured state. Combined with reported jet orientation variations, these findings support the emerging paradigm that X-ray binary jets in obscured and unobscured states have distinct propagation properties.

title: Bipolar HII regions Produced by Cloud-Cloud Collisions
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, 1 table, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We use numerical experiments to explore two possibilities: (i) that Bipolar H II Regions are the result of Cloud-Cloud Collisions (CCCs), and (ii) that -- when allowance is made for the chaotic nature of such collisions, the short duration of the bipolar phase, and different viewing angles -- a large proportion of all H II Regions might be the aftermath of CCCs. To reduce the parameter space, our experiments only consider head-on collisions between two $500$ M$_\odot$ clouds, with three different levels of turbulence, and two different collision velocities; the collision velocities define the `collision axis'. In all experiments, OB stars only condense out after a Shock-Compressed Layer has formed (perpendicular to the collision axis), and fragmented to produce a Hub Filament System, with the OB stars forming in the Hub. Ionising radiation from the OB stars excites an H II Region, which tends to expand more rapidly in directions close to the collision axis, and more slowly in directions orthogonal to the collision axis, where it encounters the dense gas of the Shock-Compressed Layer. Consequently, the H II Region may appear bipolar, for a short period during its evolution, if observed at sufficiently large angle to the collision axis. Viewed from smaller angles, the waist appears as a Bright-Rim, similar to conventional approximately spherical H II Regions. Under this circumstance, there are other metrics -- based on the extent of diffuse freefree emission, the velocity dispersion of Radio Recombination Lines, dust emission at mid-infrared wavelengths -- that might indicate the aftermath of a CCC, and establish CCCs as a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper uses numerical simulations to explore whether Bipolar H II Regions result from Cloud-Cloud Collisions (CCCs) and whether many H II Regions overall could be CCC aftermaths. Simulating head-on collisions of two 500 solar-mass clouds with varying turbulence and collision velocity, the authors find that OB stars form after a Shock-Compressed Layer fragments into a Hub Filament System. The resulting H II Region expands faster along the collision axis and slower perpendicular to it, appearing bipolar when viewed at large angles or as a bright-rimmed roughly spherical region when viewed at small angles. They propose additional observational metrics (diffuse free-free emission extent, radio recombination line velocity dispersion, mid-infrared dust emission) to identify CCC aftermaths and establish CCCs as a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.
AI.motivation: To test the hypothesis that Bipolar H II Regions arise from Cloud-Cloud Collisions and to determine whether a large fraction of all H II Regions may be the aftermath of such collisions, despite the chaotic nature, short bipolar phase duration, and varying viewing angles.
AI.method: Numerical experiments of head-on collisions between two 500 solar-mass clouds, varying turbulence (three levels) and collision velocity (two values). The collision defines an axis; simulations track the formation of shock-compressed layers, hub-filament systems, OB star formation, and the expansion of the resulting H II Region, examining how viewing angle affects observed morphology.
AI.result: OB stars form only after a Shock-Compressed Layer forms perpendicular to the collision axis and fragments into a Hub Filament System. The H II Region expands faster along the collision axis and slower perpendicular to it (where dense shocked gas lies), so it appears bipolar only for a short time and only when viewed at large angles to the collision axis. At smaller viewing angles it resembles a conventional spherical H II region with a bright rim.
AI.conclusion: Bipolar H II Regions can be explained by CCCs, and a large proportion of H II Regions may be CCC aftermaths. However, since the bipolar phase is brief and viewing-angle dependent, additional observational signatures—extent of diffuse free-free emission, radio recombination line velocity dispersion, and mid-infrared dust emission—are needed to confirm CCCs as a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

title: eRASSU J043115.8-711730: The first pulsating symbiotic super-soft X-ray source in the Magellanic Bridge
summary: The Magellanic Bridge stellar population is a relic of the tidal interaction between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. A comprehensive view of the evolution of the Bridge stellar population requires probing the compact remnants of stellar evolution, otherwise hidden at optical wavelengths. The all-sky survey conducted by the eROSITA instrument on-board the Spectrum Roentgen Gamma observatory has discovered a significant population of compact-object-powered systems in the Bridge using X-ray. The candidate super-soft source eRASSU J043115.8-711730 (hereafter J0431-71) was discovered as a part of this campaign, and we present here a deeper study of this source using XMM-Newton and SALT spectroscopy, long-term optical-infrared photometry using OGLE, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, WISE, and GAIA data. J0431-71 is a highly variable super-soft X-ray source, classified as a red giant with the GAIA color-magnitude diagram. The source exhibits: (a) a thermal X-ray spectrum with a temperature of kT$\sim$30 eV and a bright state luminosity of $3.2\times10^37$~erg~s$^{-1}$ in the 0.15-1 keV band, (b) Balmer emission lines, [Fe X] coronal line, HeII emission, and the Bowen fluorescence blend, (c) an optical and infrared periodicity of $\sim$500-560 days in phase with the X-ray-UV emission, (d) a 'redder-when-brighter' trend in the stellar emission with a $\sim$520 day period indicating a pulsating donor star. We argue that the observed spectral and temporal properties in J0431-71 are consistent with a high-accretion rate onto a white-dwarf via Roche-lobe overflow, making J0431-71 the first symbiotic source discovered in the Bridge.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a deep multi-wavelength study of the candidate super-soft X-ray source eRASSU J043115.8-711730 (J0431-71) in the Magellanic Bridge, discovered by eROSITA. Using XMM-Newton, SALT, OGLE, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, WISE, and GAIA data, the authors classify J0431-71 as a highly variable super-soft X-ray source with a thermal spectrum (kT~30 eV), showing Balmer and [Fe X] emission lines, a 500-560 day optical/IR periodicity, and a "redder-when-brighter" trend. They conclude it is the first symbiotic binary (white dwarf with Roche-lobe overflow from a pulsating red giant donor) discovered in the Magellanic Bridge.
AI.motivation: The Magellanic Bridge's stellar population is a relic of the tidal interaction between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. To fully understand its evolution, the compact remnants of stellar evolution—hidden at optical wavelengths—must be probed. The eROSITA all-sky survey discovered compact-object-powered systems in X-rays, motivating deeper follow-up studies of candidates like J0431-71 to characterize their nature.
AI.method: The authors combine X-ray spectroscopy from XMM-Newton with optical spectroscopy from SALT, and long-term optical-infrared photometry from OGLE, ATLAS, ASAS-SN, WISE, and GAIA. They analyze the X-ray spectrum for temperature and luminosity, examine emission lines (Balmer, [Fe X], HeII, Bowen fluorescence), search for periodicities in optical/IR light curves, and correlate spectral/temporal behavior across wavelengths.
AI.result: J0431-71 exhibits a thermal X-ray spectrum with kT~30 eV and bright-state luminosity of 3.2x10^37 erg/s (0.15-1 keV). It shows Balmer, [Fe X], HeII, and Bowen fluorescence emission lines. It has a ~500-560 day optical/IR periodicity in phase with X-ray-UV emission, and a "redder-when-brighter" trend with ~520 day period indicating a pulsating donor star. The source is classified as a red giant in the GAIA CMD.
AI.conclusion: The observed spectral and temporal properties are consistent with high-accretion-rate Roche-lobe overflow onto a white dwarf, identifying J0431-71 as the first symbiotic source discovered in the Magellanic Bridge.

title: Searching in HI for Massive Low Surface Brightness Galaxies: II. Completing the UGC Sample
summary: Although Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies are increasingly well studied, considerable uncertainty still exists as to both their range in properties and their evolutionary history. LSB galaxies provide a fascinating extreme in galaxy formation and evolution, allowing excellent tests of galaxy formation and evolution theories. Previously, our group successfully measured the HI gas and dynamical mass properties of 350 LSB galaxies, significantly increasing the number of known extreme LSB galaxies (massive, gas rich, etc.) in the process. Here we oresent 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope 21-cm HI line observations of a further 35 LBG galaxies, only two of which have previously published data. Of the 35, 19 were detected. This paper also includes the HI information for five additional galaxies detected accidentally (in the blank sky region or at alternative velocities), none of which has previously published HI results.

AI.tldr: This paper presents new 21-cm HI line observations of 35 Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies using the 100-m Green Bank Telescope, detecting 19 of them. Additionally, five galaxies were accidentally detected in blank sky regions or at alternative velocities, none previously published. This work extends the group's earlier sample of 350 LSB galaxies with measured HI gas and dynamical mass properties.
AI.motivation: LSB galaxies represent an extreme in galaxy formation and evolution, yet considerable uncertainty remains about their property range and evolutionary history. Expanding the sample of LSB galaxies with measured HI gas and dynamical mass properties provides improved tests of galaxy formation and evolution theories.
AI.method: The authors used the 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope to perform 21-cm HI line observations of 35 LSB galaxies, only two of which had previously published data. Of these 35 targets, 19 were detected. Additionally, five galaxies were serendipitously detected (in blank sky regions or at alternative velocities) and included in the analysis.
AI.result: 19 out of 35 targeted LSB galaxies were detected in HI. Five additional serendipitous detections were also obtained, none of which had previously published HI results. This significantly extends the known sample of extreme LSB galaxies (massive, gas-rich, etc.).
AI.conclusion: The new HI observations add 24 galaxies (19 targeted detections plus 5 serendipitous detections) to the growing census of LSB galaxy gas properties, continuing the effort to better constrain the range of properties and evolutionary histories of these extreme galaxies.

title: Comprehensive X-ray Study of Giant Radio Galaxies with XMM-Newton and Chandra
comment: Accepted for publication in JHEAp , 21 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables
summary: We present a systematic X-ray spectral analysis of 27 giant radio galaxies (GRGs) using archival \textit{XMM-Newton} and \textit{Chandra} data. Roughly 44\% of the sample show intrinsic absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H,int}} \gtrsim 10^{21}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$), while several exhibit narrow Fe K$α$ emission lines with equivalent widths up to $\sim$570 eV. Soft X-ray features are also common, including thermal plasma emission (kT$\sim 0.2$--0.8 keV) and ionized absorbers, in some cases consistent with high-velocity outflows. The photon indices are typically hard (median $ Γ\sim 1.6$), in line with radio-loud AGN. A comparison between nuclear X-ray luminosity and extended radio power shows that many sources host relatively strong X-ray cores compared to their lobes, pointing toward possible restarted nuclear activity. For 10 GRGs with published black hole masses, we explore preliminary relations with X-ray luminosity, Eddington ratio, and photon index. We find a positive trend between $M_{\rm BH}$ and $L_{2-10\,{\rm keV}}$, while Eddington ratios show no clear dependence on mass. A tentative negative relation between $λ_{\rm Edd}$ and $Γ$ hints at inefficient accretion, although confirmation will require larger samples. Overall, GRGs display diverse nuclear conditions and accretion states, supporting scenarios where obscuration, episodic or restarted activity, and low-efficiency accretion shape their long-term evolution.

AI.tldr: A systematic X-ray spectral analysis of 27 giant radio galaxies (GRGs) using XMM-Newton and Chandra data reveals diverse nuclear conditions: ~44% show intrinsic absorption, several exhibit narrow Fe Kα emission lines, common soft X-ray features include thermal plasma and ionized outflows, and hard photon indices typical of radio-loud AGN. The authors find relatively strong X-ray cores compared to lobes suggesting restarted activity, and tentative correlations between black hole mass and X-ray luminosity, with hints of low-efficiency accretion from a negative λ_Edd–Γ trend.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the nuclear X-ray properties of giant radio galaxies—objects whose X-ray nuclear conditions and accretion states remain poorly understood—in order to shed light on obscuration, episodic/restarted activity, and accretion efficiency in these extreme radio sources.
AI.method: Archival X-ray spectral analysis of 27 GRGs using XMM-Newton and Chandra data. Spectral fitting was performed to measure intrinsic absorption, Fe Kα emission lines, soft X-ray components (thermal plasma and ionized absorbers/outflows), and photon indices. Nuclear X-ray luminosities were compared to extended radio power, and relations with black hole mass, Eddington ratio, and photon index were explored for 10 sources with published BH masses.
AI.result: ~44% of the sample show intrinsic absorption (N_H,int ≳ 10^21 cm^-2); narrow Fe Kα lines with equivalent widths up to ~570 eV; thermal plasma (kT ~0.2–0.8 keV) and ionized absorbers/outflows common; hard median photon index Γ~1.6; many sources show strong X-ray cores relative to radio lobes suggesting restarted activity; a positive M_BH–L_2-10keV trend and a tentative negative λ_Edd–Γ relation were found.
AI.conclusion: GRGs exhibit diverse nuclear conditions and accretion states. Obscuration, episodic or restarted activity, and low-efficiency accretion likely shape their long-term evolution jointly. Larger samples are required to confirm the tentative accretion-related scaling relations.

title: JWST's Constraints on the Substellar IMF in NGC 2024
summary: A recent study has reported the detection of a turnover in the initial mass function (IMF) below 12 Mjup and the possible detection of a minimum mass near 3 Mjup in the heavily embedded cluster NGC 2024 (<1 Myr), which was based on a sample of brown dwarf candidates in NIRCam images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). I have used those NIRCam data in conjunction with archival spectra from JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) to constrain the substellar IMF in NGC 2024. I present NIRSpec data for 87 sources, 67 of which are within the NIRCam field. Based on those spectra and data from previous studies (e.g., X-ray emission), I have classified 45 of the NIRSpec targets as members of NGC 2024, 17 of which have spectral types indicative of brown dwarfs (M6.5-L; 13 are within NIRCam). The latter have mass estimates as low as 4 Mjup according to theoretical evolutionary models. There remain a few photometric candidates lacking spectra that extend down to the completeness limit of the images (>=2 Mjup for Ak>=1), so the minimum mass of the IMF has not been detected. It is not possible to measure a reliable substellar IMF from the NIRCam images because of the small number of brown dwarfs encompassed by them, a bias against objects at lower masses due to the high extinctions, and incompleteness at >=10 Mjup due to the saturation limit. Thus, there is no evidence in the JWST data for a turnover below 12jup.

AI.tldr: Using JWST NIRSpec archival spectra for 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field) in NGC 2024, the author classified 45 as cluster members, 17 of which are brown dwarfs (M6.5-L) with masses as low as 4 Mjup. The analysis concludes there is no evidence for a turnover or minimum mass in the substellar IMF below 12 Mjup in the JWST data, contradicting a prior claim.
AI.motivation: A recent study claimed detection of an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup and a possible minimum mass near 3 Mjup in NGC 2024 based on NIRCam photometric brown dwarf candidates. This paper aims to test that claim using spectroscopic confirmation from JWST NIRSpec archival data.
AI.method: The author combined JWST NIRCam imaging data with archival NIRSpec spectra for 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field). Sources were classified as NGC 2024 members using spectra and prior data (e.g., X-ray emission). Spectral types and mass estimates were derived via theoretical evolutionary models.
AI.result: 45 NIRSpec targets were classified as members, 17 of which are brown dwarfs (M6.5-L), 13 within the NIRCam field, with masses as low as 4 Mjup. Some photometric candidates without spectra remain down to the completeness limit (~2 Mjup for Ak>=1). The substellar IMF could not be reliably measured due to small sample size, extinction bias against low-mass objects, and saturation incompleteness at >=10 Mjup.
AI.conclusion: There is no evidence in the JWST data for an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup. The minimum mass of the IMF has not been detected, and the previously reported turnover is not supported by the spectroscopically confirmed sample.

title: The SRG/eROSITA All-Sky Survey DR2: Cumulative X-ray catalogues from the first three surveys and multi-wavelength counterparts in the western Galactic hemisphere
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A. Accompanying eROSITA-DE Data Release 2
summary: The eROSITA telescope array on board the Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission began its all-sky survey program in December 2019, scanning the sky at an approximately six-month cadence. Here, we present new catalogues of point-like and extended X-ray sources derived from the first three completed eROSITA all-sky surveys (eRASS:3), covering the western Galactic hemisphere, which Germany's eROSITA consortium holds proprietary rights for. We describe the observational strategy, data processing, and analysis pipelines. We also characterise the resulting X-ray source populations. The eRASS:3 main catalogue contains nearly two million sources, including 1,911,744 point-like and 63,796 extended sources, detected in the 0.2-2.3 keV energy band, eROSITA's most sensitive energy window. This volume has doubled the X-ray source content of eRASS1 and provides a comprehensive census of X-ray-emitting objects across diverse astrophysical classes. We also released a secondary hard catalogue of nearly 15,000 sources detected in the harder 2.3-5.0 keV energy band. In addition, we released six catalogues, three for the main sample and three for the hard sample, in which we identify and classify the optical and infrared counterparts of eRASS:3 point-like sources. This approach delivers a homogeneous, high-quality identification of mostly extragalactic X-ray emitters; for example, we estimate that approximately 88% of the 1.4 million counterparts identified within the footprints of the Legacy Survey Imaging for DESI are extragalactic sources. This work has enabled the generation of samples optimised for completeness and purity, while expanding the discovery space for rare populations. The second data release (DR2) of the SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey is a catalogue-only release, comprising the catalogues presented in this work together with an updated version of the eROSITA upper flux limit server.

The main catalogue contains nearly two million X-ray sources (1,911,744 point-like and 63,796 extended) detected in the 0.2-2.3 keV band, doubling the source content of eRASS1. A secondary hard catalogue of ~15,000 sources is also released, along with six counterpart-identification catalogues that classify optical and infrared counterparts of point-like sources, with ~88% of matched sources identified as extragalactic. This constitutes the second data release (DR2).
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive census of X-ray-emitting objects across the western Galactic hemisphere by delivering new catalogues from the first three completed eROSITA all-sky surveys, expanding the discovery space for rare populations and delivering homogeneous, high-quality identifications of X-ray sources.
AI.method: The eROSITA telescope array on board SRG scans the sky at a ~six-month cadence. The authors describe the observational strategy, data processing, and analysis pipelines used to detect point-like and extended sources in the 0.2-2.3 keV (main) and 2.3-5.0 keV (hard) energy bands. Six additional catalogues identify and classify optical/infrared counterparts of the detected point-like sources.
AI.result: The eRASS:3 main catalogue contains 1,911,744 point-like and 63,796 extended sources, doubling the X-ray source content of eRASS1. A secondary hard catalogue contains nearly 15,000 sources. Counterpart catalogues deliver homogeneous identifications, with ~88% of the 1.4 million counterparts within Legacy Survey Imaging for DESI footprints estimated to be extragalactic.
AI.conclusion: The eRASS:3 catalogues provide a major expansion of the X-ray source census and enable generation of samples optimised for completeness and purity. This catalogue-only second data release (DR2) comprises the new catalogues together with an updated eROSITA upper flux limit server.

title: X-ray Absorption Variability in NGC 1142: Another Constraint on the Nature of the Torus/Broad-Line Region in Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: The physics, geometry, and kinematics of the gas and dust surrounding the central engine of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are not well understood. In some sources, this material obscures the coronal X-ray emission, allowing its line-of-sight column density ($N_H$) to be measured. Many sources display $N_H$ variability across multiple epochs. Studying this variability can provide information about the distribution and dynamics of the obscuring material. Particularly, previous works have shown that the probability of observing $N_H$ variability increases with the number of observations available. Additionally, the observed magnitudes of the $N_H$ variability depend on the timescale between observations. In this work, we present the $N_H$ variability analysis of NGC 1142, which has a total of nine X-ray observations over $\sim20$ years, including five from a NuSTAR+XMM-Newton monitoring campaign performed in 2024-2025 and reported here for the first time. We use the physically-motivated torus models UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD to model the spectra. Our results confirm the previously observed trends, and we compare these trends to simulated obscuration curves assuming different locations and distributions of obscuring clouds.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a column density (N_H) variability analysis of the active galactic nucleus NGC 1142 using nine X-ray observations over ~20 years, including five new NuSTAR+XMM-Newton observations from a 2024-2025 monitoring campaign. The study confirms that N_H variability probability increases with observation count and that variability magnitude depends on the timescale between observations, comparing results to simulated obscuration curves from different cloud distributions.
AI.motivation: The geometry, physics, and kinematics of gas and dust obscuring AGN central engines are poorly understood. Measuring N_H variability across multiple epochs can reveal information about the distribution and dynamics of the obscuring material, informing models of the torus.
AI.method: The authors analyze nine X-ray observations of NGC 1142 spanning ~20 years, including five new NuSTAR+XMM-Newton observations from a 2024-2025 monitoring campaign reported for the first time. They model the spectra using physically-motivated torus models: UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD. They compare observed N_H variability trends to simulated obscuration curves assuming different cloud locations and distributions.
AI.result: The results confirm previously observed trends: the probability of observing N_H variability increases with the number of observations, and the magnitude of N_H variability depends on the timescale between observations. Comparisons with simulated obscuration curves constrain plausible cloud locations and distributions.
AI.conclusion: The N_H variability analysis of NGC 1142 supports existing trends and provides constraints on the distribution and dynamics of obscuring clouds around the AGN central engine through comparison with simulated obscuration curves.

title: Thermal or Non-thermal? Diffuse emission in the infall region of stacked galaxy groups
comment: Submitted to A&A, 12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table
summary: The faint infall regions surrounding the virial radius of galaxy groups remain largely unexplored due to their low X-ray surface brightness. Using the large statistical power of SRG/eROSITA survey observations, we present the first spectroscopic measurement of the intragroup medium (IGrM) in the infall regions of a large sample of low-mass galaxy groups ($M_{\rm tot}<1\times10^{14}\,M_{sun}$), extending to $\sim2\,R_{200m}$ (2.2 Mpc). Through spectral stacking of 827 nearby groups from the first eROSITA All-Sky Survey catalog, we detect diffuse emission and measure the thermodynamic properties of gas at densities previously inaccessible to X-ray observations. The stacked spectra are well described by a Gaussian differential emission measure model, yielding a temperature distribution with a mean temperature of $0.96_{-0.04}^{+0.05}$ keV and width of $0.28_{-0.10}^{+0.10}$ keV, and a metal abundance of $0.21_{-0.04}^{+0.06}$ A$_{sun}$, consistent with expectations for group outskirts. The inferred electron densities decrease from $(4.8\pm1.3)\times10^{-5}$cm$^{-3}$ at $(0.7-2)\,R_{500c}$ to $(5.5\pm2.0)\times10^{-6}$ cm$^{-3}$ at $(2-4)\,R_{500c}$, demonstrating eROSITA's ability to probe the low-density outskirts of galaxy groups. Residual emission in the spectra suggests the presence of an additional spectral component. While a secondary thermal interpretation requires an unexpectedly hot, metal-poor plasma, a non-thermal inverse Compton model provides an equally plausible explanation, contributing $\sim30\%$ of the thermal flux. Assuming that the additional component is produced by inverse Compton emission from a common population of relativistic electrons, the inferred magnetic field strength would be in the sub-$μ$G regime.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first spectroscopic measurement of the intragroup medium (IGrM) in the infall regions of low-mass galaxy groups using SRG/eROSITA survey data. By stacking spectra of 827 nearby groups, the authors detect diffuse X-ray emission extending to ~2 R200m, measuring a mean temperature of 0.96 keV, metal abundance of 0.21 Asun, and electron densities decreasing from ~4.8×10^-5 to ~5.5×10^-6 cm^-3. Residual emission suggests an additional spectral component, plausibly explained by non-thermal inverse Compton emission contributing ~30% of the thermal flux, implying sub-μG magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: The faint infall regions surrounding the virial radius of galaxy groups have remained largely unexplored because of their extremely low X-ray surface brightness. This work aims to overcome this observational barrier using the large statistical power of the eROSITA all-sky survey to probe the low-density outskirts of low-mass galaxy groups for the first time.
AI.method: The authors employ spectral stacking of 827 low-mass galaxy groups (M_tot < 10^14 Msun) from the first eROSITA All-Sky Survey catalog. Stacked spectra are modeled with a Gaussian differential emission measure (DEM) model to extract temperature distributions, metal abundances, and electron density profiles out to ~2 R200m (~2.2 Mpc). Residual emission is examined with both thermal (secondary hot, metal-poor plasma) and non-thermal (inverse Compton) interpretations.
AI.result: The stacked spectra yield a mean temperature of 0.96(+0.05/-0.04) keV with a width of 0.28 keV, a metal abundance of 0.21 Asun, and electron densities decreasing from (4.8±1.3)×10^-5 cm^-3 at (0.7-2) R500c to (5.5±2.0)×10^-6 cm^-3 at (2-4) R500c. Residual emission indicates an additional component; a non-thermal inverse Compton interpretation is equally plausible as a secondary hot thermal component, contributing ~30% of the thermal flux and implying sub-μG magnetic field strengths.

The findings open new avenues for studying the thermodynamics of the IGrM in group outskirts and the potential detection of non-thermal emission, with implications for magnetic field strengths in the circumgroup medium.

title: Characterizing the disruption of Böotes III: a missing link in the Galactic halo?
summary: The Böotes III (Boo3) dwarf galaxy has long been suspected of being the progenitor of Styx, a ~50°-long stellar stream that was simultaneously discovered in the same region of sky. Boo3's diffuse morphology, large velocity dispersion, small pericenter, and excess of candidate stars at large radii suggest it is undergoing active tidal disruption. A link to Styx is therefore logical; however, a clear connection between these structures has not yet been clearly demonstrated. Here, we re-examine the Boo3-Styx association by searching for Boo3's tidal debris using a combination of Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band imaging with CFHT/MegaCam, and stellar tracer catalogues of blue horizontal branch and red giant branch stars. We also conduct a broad search for a putative stream using matched filter techniques applied to SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2. Despite our extensive search, we find no observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx. Furthermore, our results suggest that either Boo3's extended substructure is too diffuse to be detected with current data, or that its particular orbit may have erased a coherent tidal signature. Boo3 thus remains an enigmatic system, and exemplifies the need for spectroscopic follow-up to properly disentangle the nature between this faint Milky Way satellite and nearby stream.

AI.tldr: Astronomers re-examine the hypothesized association between the Böotes III (Boo3) dwarf galaxy and the Styx stellar stream using Gaia, CFHT/MegaCam CaHK imaging, stellar tracer catalogues, and matched-filter searches of SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2, finding no observational evidence linking the two structures.
AI.motivation: Boo3 has features suggesting active tidal disruption and was suspected to be the progenitor of the ~50°-long Styx stream, but a clear connection had not been demonstrated.
AI.method: Combined Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band imaging with CFHT/MegaCam, blue horizontal branch and red giant branch stellar tracer catalogues, plus matched-filter techniques applied to SDSS DR17 and DELVE DR2 for a broad stream search.
AI.result: No observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx was found despite the extensive search.
AI.conclusion: Boo3's extended substructure may be too diffuse for current data, or its orbit may have erased a coherent tidal signature; Boo3 remains enigmatic and requires spectroscopic follow-up to disentangle its nature relative to the nearby stream.

title: Tidal Disruption Events with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/TaoAn03. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) and related nuclear transients probe jet launching, disk formation and circularization, particle acceleration, and the circumnuclear medium (CNM). However, the small fraction of events launching relativistic jets, the weak or delayed radio emission of many thermal TDEs, and the black-hole demographics of galactic nuclei remain poorly understood. SKA, with microJy sensitivity, wide bandwidth, long baselines, rapid response, and commensal surveys across 50-350 MHz (SKA-Low) and 0.35-15.4 GHz (SKA-Mid), will transform this field. Its sensitivity, frequency coverage, and very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) capability will extend radio calorimetry from a few well-studied nearby events to volume-limited samples of non-relativistic outflows. The SKA will bring off-axis and mildly relativistic jets into routine reach, trace CNM density profiles through the evolution of the low-frequency synchrotron turnover, and localize faint off-nuclear transients with sub-arcsecond precision. These data will constrain jet incidence, energetics, geometry, and magnetization, map the CNM through shock interactions, test links to changing-look active galactic nuclei (AGN) and high-energy neutrinos, and identify off-nuclear events associated with recoiling supermassive or intermediate-mass black holes. We discuss the benefits of commensal surveys, rapid triggering, and SKA-VLBI, and provide predictions based on the projected performance of AA* and AA4. SKA will shift TDE radio studies from detailed case-by-case studies to population-scale inference, advancing studies of jet physics and black-hole demographics.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will transform studies of tidal disruption events (TDEs) and related nuclear transients, moving the field from case-by-case radio observations to population-scale inference through its microJy sensitivity, wide frequency coverage (50 MHz–15.4 GHz), VLBI capability, and rapid response/commensal surveying.
AI.motivation: Current understanding of TDEs and nuclear transients is limited by the small fraction of events launching relativistic jets, weak or delayed radio emission in many thermal TDEs, and poorly constrained black-hole demographics in galactic nuclei. These open questions motivate the need for a transformative observational facility.
AI.method: The paper presents a forward-looking analysis of SKA capabilities (SKA-Low 50–350 MHz and SKA-Mid 0.35–15.4 GHz), including commensal surveys, rapid triggering, and SKA-VLBI, and provides predictions based on projected performance of the AA* and AA4 configurations.
AI.result: The SKA will extend radio calorimetry from a few nearby events to volume-limited samples, bring off-axis and mildly relativistic jets into routine reach, trace CNM density profiles via low-frequency synchrotron turnover, localize off-nuclear transients with sub-arcsecond precision, and enable population-scale constraints on jet incidence, energetics, geometry, and magnetization.
AI.conclusion: SKA will shift TDE radio studies from detailed case-by-case analysis to population-scale inference, advancing jet physics and black-hole demographics, while linking TDEs to changing-look AGN, high-energy neutrinos, and recoiling or intermediate-mass black holes.

title: Thermal Breaking of the I-Love Universality for Hot White Dwarfs
summary: The universal I-Love-Q relations for compact stars have significant applications in gravitational-wave astronomy, but thermal effects can break these relations in low-mass white dwarfs. In this work, we employ the stellar evolution code MESA to construct realistic models of $0.15 \, M_{\odot}$ helium-core and $0.6 \, M_{\odot}$ carbon-oxygen core white dwarfs at various temperatures. By utilizing the Clairaut-Radau equation, we quantitatively extract the radial variation of the eccentricity of internal isodensity surfaces. Our numerical results demonstrate that higher central temperatures amplify the eccentricity variation, causing the I-Love relations to deviate from the zero-temperature Chandrasekhar model, whereas subsequent cooling restores them. This confirms that the temperature-induced violation of the universal relations is fundamentally driven by the loss of self-similarity in isodensity surfaces, providing key insights into the applicability conditions of I-Love-Q relations in compact objects.

AI.tldr: The paper uses MESA stellar evolution code to model low-mass white dwarfs (0.15 Msun helium-core and 0.6 Msun CO-core) at various temperatures, showing that thermal effects break I-Love-Q universal relations by altering internal isodensity surface eccentricity, with cooling restoring the relations.
AI.motivation: The I-Love-Q universal relations are important for gravitational-wave astronomy, but it is unclear whether thermal effects in low-mass white dwarfs violate these relations and under what conditions they hold.
AI.method: The authors use the MESA stellar evolution code to construct realistic white dwarf models at different temperatures, then employ the Clairaut-Radau equation to quantitatively extract the radial variation of eccentricity of internal isodensity surfaces.
AI.result: Higher central temperatures amplify eccentricity variation and cause I-Love relations to deviate from the zero-temperature Chandrasekhar model, while subsequent cooling restores the universal relations.
AI.conclusion: Temperature-induced violation of universal relations is driven by the loss of self-similarity in isodensity surfaces, providing insight into the applicability conditions of I-Love-Q relations in compact objects.

title: Impact of Kaon Condensation on the Thermal Evolution of the CCO in HESS J1731--347 Supernova Remnant
summary: Recent analyses of the central compact object in the HESS J1731--347 supernova remnant suggest an unusual combination of a low mass and small radius, while its thermal emission indicates a relatively high surface temperature at its estimated age. Reconciling these structural and thermal properties within a unified theoretical framework may provide important constraints on the equation of state and composition of dense matter. In this work, we investigate the thermal consequences of negatively charged kaon condensation, an exotic phase that softens the equation of state and facilitate the reproduction of the inferred bulk properties of HESS J1731--347. We find that the onset of kaon condensation strongly accelerates the thermal evolution, leading to surface temperature substantially below the observationally inferred range. Within the adopted cooling framework, kaon condensation therefore cannot simultaneously account for the structural and thermal properties of HESS J1731--347.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether negatively charged kaon condensation, an exotic phase that softens the equation of state and helps reproduce the structural properties of the central compact object in HESS J1731--347, can also explain its observed surface temperature. The authors find that kaon condensation accelerates thermal evolution too strongly, producing surface temperatures well below the observed range, thus ruling out kaon condensation as a unified explanation.
AI.motivation: The central compact object in the HESS J1731--347 supernova remnant exhibits an unusual combination of low mass, small radius, and high surface temperature for its estimated age. Reconciling these properties within a unified theoretical framework would provide important constraints on the equation of state and composition of dense matter. Negatively charged kaon condensation is a candidate exotic phase that softens the equation of state and could reproduce the inferred bulk properties.
AI.method: The authors investigate the thermal consequences of negatively charged kaon condensation within a cooling framework. They model the thermal evolution of the star incorporating kaon condensation and compare the resulting surface temperatures with the observationally inferred range for HESS J1731--347.
AI.result: The onset of kaon condensation strongly accelerates the thermal evolution of the neutron star, causing its surface temperature to fall substantially below the observationally inferred range. Thus, within the adopted cooling framework, kaon condensation cannot simultaneously account for both the structural and thermal properties of HESS J1731--347.
AI.conclusion: Kaon condensation, although capable of softening the equation of state to match the structural properties of HESS J1731--347, is excluded as a viable explanation because it drives the thermal evolution too rapidly, producing surface temperatures inconsistent with observations. This rules out kaon condensation as a unified framework for this object.

title: High-mass binary black hole mergers from detailed binary evolution models
summary:
Gravitational-wave observations reveal a population of binary black hole (BBH) mergers with primary masses above ${\sim}40\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, extending into and potentially beyond the pair-instability mass gap, with a possibly flat mass-ratio and broader χ_\mathrm{eff} distribution. We investigate whether super-Eddington accretion during stable mass transfer in isolated binary evolution can produce BBH mergers consistent with these properties across primary BH mass, mass-ratio, and χ_\mathrm{eff} distributions. Using POSYDON, we simulate BBH merger populations with primary BH masses above ${\sim}40\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, under three BH accretion efficiencies: Eddington-limited, GRRMHD-informed, and fully conservative. We additionally vary the natal kick strength, including strong kicks at high BH masses.
  We find that super-Eddington accretion does not suppress BBH mergers in the high-mass regime. Fully-conservative accretion leads to an increase of BBH mergers in POSYDON with a strong kick-independent peak at $χ_\mathrm{eff}=0.6$ and a sharp mass-ratio peak at $q\sim0.5$, whereas observations favor $χ_\mathrm{eff}=0.0$ and a flatter mass-ratio distribution. The GRRMHD-informed and Eddington-limited accretion are compatible with the observed primary BH mass and mass ratio distribution, but require natal kicks to populate negative χ_\mathrm{eff}.
  A joint analysis of the primary BH mass, mass ratio, and χ_\mathrm{eff} distributions provides strong constraints on binary evolution physics, and disfavor fully-conservative BH accretion as the dominant formation mechanism for high-mass BBH mergers. The Eddington-limited and GRRMHD-informed prescriptions with modest kicks can explain part of the high-mass population, but an additional formation channel is still needed to account for the high fraction of negative χ_\mathrm{eff} systems and high secondary BH spins.

AI.tldr: This study uses POSYDON binary evolution simulations to test whether super-Eddington accretion during stable mass transfer can explain the properties of high-mass (>40 M⊙) binary black hole mergers. Fully-conservative accretion is disfavored as the dominant formation mechanism, while Eddington-limited and GRRMHD-informed prescriptions with modest natal kicks can explain part of the population but cannot account for the observed negative χ_eff systems and high secondary BH spins.
AI.motivation: Gravitational-wave observations have revealed a population of BBH mergers with primary masses above ~40 M⊙, extending into the pair-instability mass gap, with possibly flat mass-ratio and broader effective spin distributions. The authors aim to test whether super-Eddington accretion during stable mass transfer in isolated binary evolution can produce BBH mergers consistent with these observed properties.
AI.method: Using the POSYDON population synthesis code, the authors simulate BBH merger populations with primary BH masses above ~40 M⊙ under three BH accretion efficiency prescriptions: Eddington-limited, GRRMHD-informed, and fully conservative. They additionally vary the natal kick strength, including strong kicks at high BH masses, and perform a joint analysis of primary BH mass, mass ratio, and χ_eff distributions.
AI.result: Super-Eddington accretion does not suppress BBH mergers in the high-mass regime. Fully-conservative accretion produces a strong kick-independent peak at χ_eff=0.6 and a sharp mass-ratio peak at q~0.5, which is inconsistent with observations favoring χ_eff=0.0 and a flatter mass-ratio distribution. GRRMHD-informed and Eddington-limited accretion match observed primary mass and mass-ratio distributions but require natal kicks to populate negative χ_eff. Joint analysis disfavors fully-conservative accretion as the dominant formation channel.
AI.conclusion: Eddington-limited and GRRMHD-informed accretion prescriptions with modest natal kicks can explain part of the high-mass BBH population, but an additional formation channel is still required to account for the high fraction of negative χ_eff systems and high secondary BH spins observed by gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Comparative Periodogram Analysis of 22 Years of Super-Kamiokande Solar $^{8}\mathrm{B}$ Neutrino Data: Classical, Phase-Based, and Information Theoretic Methods
summary: Solar $^8\mathrm{B}$ neutrinos offer a unique probe of solar interior dynamics and neutrino electromagnetic properties. We present a systematic, multi-method periodogram analysis of the 22-year Super-Kamiokande solar neutrino dataset (1996--2018), comparing nine algorithms. Through hierarchical temporal segmentation, we disentangle astrophysical signals from detector systematics. The Generalized Lomb-Scargle (GLS) method provides the most statistically robust detections by correctly handling heteroscedastic uncertainties, whereas classical Lomb-Scargle systematically underestimates significance. The Lafler--Kinman method generally fails, whereas independent algorithms like MHAOV and PDM1 recover consistent periodicities, providing vital cross-validation. In pre-2001 and SK-I data, seven algorithms provide \textit{weak evidence} ($\ln B > 0$) for a $\sim 38.8$ d periodicity. However, this signal is entirely absent in the highest-statistics SK-IV modified flux data, where the Bayes factor decisively favors the null model ($\ln B \ll -5$), indicating it is a transient feature of the early low-statistics era. Conversely, a $\sim 24.3$ d signal in post-2001 raw flux is decisively rejected by the Bayesian framework and vanishes in modified flux, confirming its seasonal systematic origin. Furthermore, no evidence is found for an $\sim 11$-year solar cycle modulation, yielding a stringent amplitude upper limit of $<0.2\%$ of the mean flux. By highlighting the stark contrast between frequentist significance and Bayesian model selection ($\ln B$) in low signal-to-noise regimes, we establish a rigorous, multi-metric best-practice framework for periodicity searches. This work provides a direct methodological blueprint for next-generation observatories like Hyper-Kamiokande and JUNO.

AI.tldr: A multi-method periodogram analysis of 22 years of Super-Kamiokande solar 8B neutrino data (1996–2018) using nine algorithms finds that the Generalized Lomb-Scargle method is most robust, identifies a transient ~38.8 d periodicity confined to early low-statistics data, rejects a ~24.3 d signal as a seasonal systematic, finds no ~11-year solar cycle modulation (<0.2% amplitude upper limit), and establishes a Bayesian-vs-frequentist multi-metric framework for periodicity searches.
AI.motivation: Solar 8B neutrinos probe solar interior dynamics and neutrino electromagnetic properties, yet robust periodicity searches in long-baseline solar neutrino data require systematic comparison of analysis methods to disentangle genuine astrophysical signals from detector systematics and to establish reliable detection criteria in low signal-to-noise regimes.
AI.method: A hierarchical temporal segmentation of the 22-year Super-Kamiokande dataset is performed, comparing nine periodogram algorithms including Generalized Lomb-Scargle (GLS), classical Lomb-Scargle, Lafler-Kinman, MHAOV, and PDM1. Both frequentist significance testing and Bayesian model selection (via Bayes factors, ln B) are applied, with cross-validation across independent algorithms and data sub-phases (pre-2001, SK-I, post-2001, SK-IV modified flux).
AI.result: GLS provides the most statistically robust detections by properly handling heteroscedastic uncertainties; classical Lomb-Scargle underestimates significance while Lafler-Kinman generally fails. Seven algorithms give weak evidence (ln B > 0) for a ~38.8 d periodicity in pre-2001/SK-I data, but this is entirely absent in SK-IV modified flux (ln B ≪ −5), indicating it is transient. A ~24.3 d post-2001 signal is decisively rejected by Bayesian analysis and vanishes in modified flux, confirming a seasonal systematic. No ~11-year modulation is found, with an amplitude upper limit <0.2% of the mean flux.
AI.conclusion: Frequentist significance and Bayesian model selection can starkly disagree in low signal-to-noise regimes, and the study establishes a rigorous multi-metric best-practice framework for periodicity searches. The methodological blueprint is directly applicable to next-generation observatories such as Hyper-Kamiokande and JUNO.

title: The First Measurement of Jet Collimation Profiles in an X-ray Binary: the Case of SS 433
comment: This is a revised manuscript submitted to ApJL
summary: While significant progress has been achieved in active galactic nuclei (AGN), jet collimation profiles in X-ray binaries (XRBs) have not been directly measured. Here we report the first measurement of jet collimation profiles in an XRB using very long baseline interferometry data from SS 433. The approaching jet exhibits a well-constrained quasi-parabolic profile in the 1995 and 1998 data, whereas the prominent local oscillations present in the 2000 jet-width measurements preclude a robust characterization of the jet collimation profile. Nevertheless, the 2000 data suggest that the intrinsic jet opening angle decreases gradually from $\sim 20^\circ$ at 8$\times 10^{14}$ cm to $\sim 3^\circ$ at $9\times 10^{15}$ cm (deprojected), providing evidence for progressive jet collimation. The width and opening angle of the receding jet are also presented, although their interpretation is limited by the free--free absorption effect. In addition, we measure the frequency-dependent core positions at four bands and derive a core-shift relation. These results establish SS 433 as the first XRB in which jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift relation are constrained.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first direct measurement of jet collimation profiles in an X-ray binary (XRB) using VLBI data from SS 433. The approaching jet shows a quasi-parabolic profile in 1995/1998 data, the 2000 data suggest progressive collimation (opening angle decreasing from ~20° to ~3°), and frequency-dependent core positions yield a core-shift relation—establishing SS 433 as the first XRB with constrained jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift relation.
AI.motivation: While jet collimation profiles have been extensively studied in active galactic nuclei (AGN), they have never been directly measured in X-ray binaries (XRBs). This work aims to fill that gap by measuring the jet collimation profile in the XRB SS 433 using very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) data.
AI.method: The study uses very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations of SS 433 from 1995, 1998, and 2000 epochs. Jet widths are measured to derive collimation profiles for both the approaching and receding jets, and the intrinsic opening angle as a function of deprojected radius is computed. Frequency-dependent core positions across four frequency bands are used to derive a core-shift relation.
AI.result: The approaching jet shows a well-constrained quasi-parabolic profile in 1995 and 1998, while 2000 data exhibit local oscillations precluding robust profile characterization but suggesting a gradual decrease in intrinsic opening angle from ~20° at 8×10^14 cm to ~3° at 9×10^15 cm, providing evidence for progressive jet collimation. Receding jet width and opening angle are also presented but limited by free-free absorption. A core-shift relation is derived from four-band frequency-dependent core positions.
AI.conclusion: SS 433 is established as the first X-ray binary in which jet collimation, opening-angle evolution, and core-shift relation are all constrained, providing a crucial XRB counterpart to AGN jet collimation studies.

title: Multiwavelength study of supernova remnants in the Circinus constellation with SRG/eROSITA
summary: Supernova remnants (SNRs) are key tracers of stellar feedback and the chemical and dynamical evolution of the interstellar medium. However, identifying SNRs in complex regions remains challenging, particularly when only archival multi-wavelength data are available. We aim to search for previously unrecognized SNR candidates in the Circinus constellation by combining optical imaging, radio continuum data, and available SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey X-ray observations, to provide a prioritized list of targets for future confirmation. Candidate remnants were classified according to the strength of the combined diagnostics. This joint analysis yields improved constraints on the morphology and spectral properties of known remnants in the region, including MSH 15-52 and G320.6- 1.6. In addition, we identify a new promising SNR candidate, G320.2-3.6. Our study provides a first multi-wavelength search of SNR candidates in the Circinus region. In addition to G320.2-3.6, three objects (G319.8-2.0, G321.8-1.1, and G320.5-1.8) emerge as promising targets for follow-up radio, spectroscopic optical, and deeper, spatially resolved X-ray observations to confirm their nature.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-wavelength search for previously unrecognized supernova remnant (SNR) candidates in the Circinus constellation by combining optical imaging, radio continuum data, and SRG/eROSITA X-ray observations. The study identifies a new promising SNR candidate (G320.2-3.6) and three additional targets for follow-up confirmation, while also improving constraints on known remnants like MSH 15-52 and G320.6-1.6.
AI.motivation: Identifying supernova remnants remains challenging in complex regions, particularly when only archival multi-wavelength data are available. The authors aim to discover previously unrecognized SNR candidates in the Circinus constellation, where no systematic multi-wavelength search had been conducted.
AI.method: The study combines multi-wavelength observations—optical imaging, radio continuum data, and SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey X-ray data—to search for SNR candidates. Candidate remnants were classified according to the strength of combined diagnostics across these wavelength regimes.
AI.result: The joint analysis improves constraints on the morphology and spectral properties of known remnants (MSH 15-52 and G320.6-1.6) and identifies a new promising SNR candidate, G320.2-3.6. Three additional objects (G319.8-2.0, G321.8-1.1, and G320.5-1.8) were flagged as promising targets for follow-up verification.
