The newly identified candidate G320.2-3.6 and three other objects warrant follow-up radio, spectroscopic optical, and deeper spatially resolved X-ray observations to confirm their nature as supernova remnants.

title: Estimating amplitude of matter density fluctuations in solar and supernova models using neutrino flavor evolution
summary: Neutrinos can undergo substantial flavor evolution between their production in astrophysical sources-such as the Sun and core-collapse supernovae-and their subsequent detection in terrestrial detectors. This flavor evolution is strongly influenced by the environment that the neutrinos interact with, making them useful astrophysical messengers capable of potentially carrying information about the properties of the source wherein they are produced. In this work, we apply the framework of statistical data assimilation (SDA) in order to ascertain the extent to which a neutrino signal at detection may contain information about matter density fluctuations along their path from the source. Using simplified models of neutrino flavor evolution and propagation in the sun and in a core-collapse supernova (CCSN), we find that the SDA method is able to extract information about the amplitude of density fluctuations in both the solar and CCSN scenarios, with the method showing relatively greater reliability in the solar neutrino case. Nonetheless, even in the CCSN neutrino model, the method proved effective at high fluctuation amplitudes

AI.tldr: This paper applies statistical data assimilation (SDA) to determine whether neutrino signals detected on Earth can reveal information about matter density fluctuations along their propagation path from astrophysical sources like the Sun and core-collapse supernovae. Using simplified models, the SDA method successfully extracts fluctuation amplitude information in both scenarios, with greater reliability for solar neutrinos, though still effective for supernova neutrinos at high fluctuation amplitudes.
AI.motivation: Neutrinos undergo flavor evolution influenced by their environment, making them potential astrophysical messengers. The authors aim to determine whether detected neutrino signals can encode information about matter density fluctuations along their propagation path from sources such as the Sun and core-collapse supernovae.
AI.method: The authors apply statistical data assimilation (SDA) to simplified models of neutrino flavor evolution and propagation in the Sun and in a core-collapse supernova (CCSN), testing the method's ability to extract information about the amplitude of matter density fluctuations.
AI.result: The SDA method successfully extracts information about density fluctuation amplitudes in both the solar and CCSN scenarios. It demonstrates relatively greater reliability in the solar neutrino case; however, it remains effective in the CCSN model at high fluctuation amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: Statistical data assimilation is a viable technique for extracting environmental (density fluctuation) information from detected neutrino signals, particularly promising for solar neutrinos and effective for CCSN neutrinos under high-fluctuation conditions.

title: Binary neutron stars in the next-generation era: Multi-messenger detection prospects and constraints on the equation of state, mass distribution, and cosmology
summary: Next-generation gravitational-wave (GW) observatories will provide crucial insights into the nature of neutron star (NS) matter and the cosmological expansion history. We estimate the number of multi-messenger detections from binary neutron stars (BNS) with the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE), and project the resulting constraints on the equation of state (EOS), BNS mass distribution, and cosmology via joint hierarchical Bayesian inference. Assuming a local merger rate of 106.6 Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$ and considering two different mass functions, a narrow one centred around 1.4 $M_\odot$ and a wide one ranging between 1.1--2 $M_\odot$, we find that for ET, our mock follow-up algorithm results in at least $\sim40$ and up to $\sim100$ successfully identified electromagnetic counterparts per year, depending on the detector layout and mass distribution. In a joint network with CE, the number of multi-messenger detections can range from $\sim 200$ to $\sim500$. Additionally, several more afterglows from gamma-ray bursts or KNe could be found with dedicated late-time observations. Based on the identified multi-messenger events, we perform an injection campaign to hierarchically constrain the EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology in a fully Bayesian framework. Focussing on ET alone, we show how in an ideal scenario, GW signals, KNe, and host galaxy redshifts can constrain the canonical NS radius $R_{1.4}$ within $\sim 0.2$ km and the Hubble constant $H_0$ within $\sim 1$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, while recovering the essential features of the mass distribution. By comparing inference results that rely solely on GW data and those that incorporate light curve information, we find that while KN light-curve posteriors have a negligible impact on the EOS constraints, they can benefit the inference of cosmological parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper estimates the number of multi-messenger detections from binary neutron star mergers with next-generation gravitational-wave observatories (Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer) and projects their ability to jointly constrain the neutron star equation of state, mass distribution, and cosmology via hierarchical Bayesian inference. The authors find ~40-100 multi-messenger detections per year for ET alone and ~200-500 for a joint ET+CE network, and show that in ideal scenarios the canonical NS radius R1.4 can be constrained to ~0.2 km and H0 to ~1 km/s/Mpc.
AI.motivation: Next-generation gravitational-wave observatories will provide crucial insights into the nature of neutron star matter and the cosmological expansion history. The authors aim to quantify the scientific return of multi-messenger observations with these future facilities to guide detector design and observational strategy.
AI.method: The authors simulate BNS merger detections assuming a local merger rate of 106.6 Gpc^-3 yr^-1, consider two mass functions (narrow centered at 1.4 Msun, wide 1.1-2 Msun), run mock follow-up algorithms to identify electromagnetic counterparts, and perform injection campaigns for joint hierarchical Bayesian inference of the EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology using GW signals, kilonova light curves, and host galaxy redshifts.
AI.result: ET alone yields ~40-100 successfully identified electromagnetic counterparts per year depending on detector layout and mass distribution, while a joint ET+CE network yields ~200-500. In ideal scenarios, the canonical NS radius R1.4 can be constrained to ~0.2 km and H0 to ~1 km/s/Mpc. KN light-curve posteriors have negligible impact on EOS constraints but benefit cosmological parameter inference.
AI.conclusion: Next-generation GW observatories will enable large multi-messenger BNS samples that can jointly constrain the EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology with high precision, with kilonova light curves primarily aiding cosmology rather than EOS inference.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Tidal Disruption Event Classification : A Host-Agnostic Probabilistic Random Forest Approach
summary: The classification of Tidal Disruption Events in large-scale photometric surveys is challenging because deterministic machine learning models produce overconfident misclassifications under varying data quality and low signal-to-noise conditions. Existing lightcurve-based approaches fail to incorporate measurement uncertainties, consequently generating brittle outputs. We present a host-agnostic, uncertainty-aware classification framework using a Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF). Our pipeline extracts 11 characteristic features from nuclear transients in the ZTF alert stream, including rise and decay timescales, blackbody temperature evolution, and pre-transient variability metrics. Relying exclusively on photometric data without host galaxy information ensures effectiveness for the faint transient population expected from the Rubin Observatory. The PRF, which treats feature measurements as distributions, was evaluated against XGBoost through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation. It yields higher stability and robustness for ambiguous candidates than XGBoost. The two classifiers occupy complementary regimes. XGBoost achieves higher recall in balanced and high-precision scenarios, where its rigid decision boundaries efficiently isolate TDE-like sources, while PRF rejects more false positives by penalizing sources with large feature uncertainties. Applying this framework to archival data identified 11 new candidate TDEs from the unclassified population and 3 potential photometric TDEs within existing training labels previously misclassified as supernovae or active galactic nuclei. This work demonstrates that TDEs can be reliably identified using photometric lightcurve features, providing a host-independent framework. Uncertainty-aware, probabilistic classifiers are essential for the Rubin era to prevent the overconfident misclassifications inherent in deterministic models at low signal-to-noise.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an uncertainty-aware Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF) framework for classifying Tidal Disruption Events (TDEs) in large-scale photometric surveys, using 11 host-agnostic lightcurve features from ZTF alert data. Compared to XGBoost via Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation, the PRF is more stable and robust for ambiguous candidates, rejecting more false positives under uncertainty. Applied to archival data, it identified 11 new TDE candidates and 3 previously misclassified TDEs, demonstrating the critical need for probabilistic classifiers in the Rubin Observatory era.
AI.motivation: Deterministic machine learning models produce overconfident misclassifications of TDEs under varying data quality and low signal-to-noise conditions, and existing lightcurve-based approaches fail to incorporate measurement uncertainties, making their outputs brittle. A host-independent, uncertainty-aware classification framework is needed for the faint transient population expected from upcoming surveys like the Rubin Observatory.
AI.method: The pipeline extracts 11 characteristic features from nuclear transients in the ZTF alert stream, including rise/decay timescales, blackbody temperature evolution, and pre-transient variability metrics. It uses a Probabilistic Random Forest (PRF) that treats feature measurements as probability distributions, evaluated against XGBoost through Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation.
AI.result: The PRF yields higher stability and robustness for ambiguous candidates than XGBoost, rejecting more false positives by penalizing sources with large feature uncertainties, while XGBoost achieves higher recall in balanced and high-precision scenarios. Application to archival data identified 11 new candidate TDEs from the unclassified population and 3 potential photometric TDEs previously misclassified as supernovae or AGN.
AI.conclusion: TDEs can be reliably identified using photometric lightcurve features in a host-independent manner, and uncertainty-aware probabilistic classifiers are essential for the Rubin era to prevent the overconfident misclassifications inherent in deterministic models at low signal-to-noise.

title: Same explosion, many faces: numerical modeling reveals viewing angle as a driver of diversity for core-collapse SNe in binary systems
comment: 19 pages, 12 figures, submitted to AAS journals. Comments are welcome
summary: Observable properties of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) depend sensitively on the circumstellar material (CSM) formed by pre-explosion mass loss from the progenitor star. Since a large fraction of CCSN progenitors reside in binaries, both the progenitor structure and surrounding CSM can be significantly impacted by binary interaction. Yet, its impact on the observed CCSN landscape remains poorly constrained. In this work, we investigate CCSNe from binary systems undergoing stable Roche lobe overflow. We construct a suite of binary evolution models in \texttt{MESA} with a fixed initial primary mass ($16M_{\odot}$), exploring secondary masses in the range $12-15M_{\odot}$ and initial orbital periods $>500$ days. We generate three-dimensional (3D) CSM structures from the resulting mass-loss histories and orbital dynamics, extract angle-dependent density profiles along three lines of sight, and compute multi-band light curves with the radiation-hydrodynamics code \texttt{Stella}. We find that binary-driven CSM develops highly aspherical morphologies, governed by the orbital period and the mass ratio. Interaction between SN ejecta and this structured medium produces pronounced viewing-angle dependence in the light curves, with peak luminosities differing by factors of $\sim5$ and late-time $B-V$ colors varying by $\sim1.5$ mag depending on observer orientation. We further show that interpreting such events with one-dimensional frameworks assuming isolated progenitors and spherical winds can introduce biases up to $50\%$ for inferred explosion properties and $>200\%$ for inferred mass-loss rates. Our results are consistent with a substantial fraction of interacting Type II SN diversity arising from binary-shaped asymmetric CSM and viewing-angle effects, motivating multidimensional approaches to interpreting these transients.

AI.motivation: A large fraction of CCSN progenitors reside in binaries, and binary interaction can significantly impact both the progenitor structure and surrounding CSM. However, the impact of binary-driven asymmetric CSM on the observed CCSN landscape remains poorly constrained, motivating a systematic investigation.
AI.method: The authors constructed a suite of binary evolution models in MESA with a fixed initial primary mass (16 solar masses), exploring secondary masses 12-15 solar masses and initial orbital periods >500 days. They generated 3D CSM structures from mass-loss histories and orbital dynamics, extracted angle-dependent density profiles along three lines of sight, and computed multi-band light curves using the radiation-hydrodynamics code Stella.

SN ejecta interaction with this structured medium produces pronounced viewing-angle dependence: peak luminosities differ by factors of ~5 and late-time B-V colors vary by ~1.5 mag depending on observer orientation. Interpreting such events with 1D frameworks assuming isolated progenitors and spherical winds can introduce biases up to 50% for inferred explosion properties and >200% for inferred mass-loss rates.
AI.conclusion: A substantial fraction of interacting Type II SN diversity may arise from binary-shaped asymmetric CSM and viewing-angle effects, motivating multidimensional approaches to interpreting these transients rather than relying on standard 1D spherical frameworks.

title: Search for gravitational waves associated with high-energy neutrinos detected by IceCube during the third observing run of LIGO-Virgo
summary: We search for generic gravitational-wave transients associated with high-energy neutrinos detected by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory during the third Observing Run (O3) of Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA. We perform an unmodeled, targeted search, which is sensitive to gravitational-wave signals weaker than those reported in real time or in the gravitional-wave transient catalog, and can thus uncover coincidences missed by typical neutrino follow-up searches. We find no statistically significant gravitational-wave signal and set lower bounds on the distance of possible gravitational-wave sources for different emission models.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an unmodeled, targeted search for generic gravitational-wave transients associated with high-energy neutrinos from IceCube during LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA's third Observing Run (O3). No statistically significant gravitational-wave signals were found, and lower bounds on source distances were set for various emission models.
AI.motivation: To uncover coincident gravitational-wave and neutrino events that might be missed by typical real-time or catalog-based follow-up searches, by using a more sensitive unmodeled targeted search approach.
AI.method: An unmodeled, targeted gravitational-wave search is performed, correlated with high-energy neutrino detections from IceCube during O3. The search is designed to be sensitive to gravitational-wave signals weaker than those reported in real time or in the transient catalog.
AI.result: No statistically significant gravitational-wave signal was found. Lower bounds on the distances of possible gravitational-wave sources were set for different emission models.
AI.conclusion: The search found no evidence for coincident gravitational-wave and neutrino emission, and the derived distance lower bounds place constraints on possible source populations.

title: Spinning down neutron-star merger remnants with the Tayler-Spruit dynamo: Global simulations reveal the formation of massive disks and neutron-rich ejecta
summary: Magnetic-field amplification and angular momentum (AM) transport critically shape the secular evolution, lifetime, and electromagnetic signatures of binary neutron-star merger remnants. While the magnetorotational instability can operate in the outer negative-shear regions of the neutron-star remnant and accretion disk, the positive-shear, stably stratified core may instead be susceptible to the Tayler-Spruit dynamo. We present the first global, long-term general-relativistic neutrino-radiation magnetohydrodynamics simulations of a neutron-star merger remnant incorporating the unresolved Tayler-Spruit dynamo through a new mean-field dynamo subgrid prescription. Our axisymmetric simulations starting from a realistic merger remnant show that the Tayler-Spruit dynamo is primarily active in high-latitude regions of the remnant core. The resulting Maxwell stresses redistribute AM on a spin-down timescale of a few hundred milliseconds, substantially flattening the core rotation profile and transferring mass and AM from the outer remnant into the disk. This produces a more massive, extended, and strongly magnetized disk with a low electron fraction, leading to substantially more neutron-rich ejecta. Our results demonstrate that currently unmodelled Tayler-Spruit dynamo action can qualitatively alter the rotational evolution, collapse prospects, disk formation, and multi-messenger signatures of long-lived neutron-star merger remnants.

AI.tldr: First global GR neutrino-radiation MHD simulations of a neutron-star merger remnant incorporating the unresolved Tayler-Spruit dynamo via a new mean-field subgrid prescription show that this dynamo is active in the high-latitude core, flattens the rotation profile on ~100ms timescales, produces a more massive, extended, strongly magnetized low-electron-fraction disk, and substantially alters ejecta properties and multi-messenger signatures.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the previously unmodelled Tayler-Spruit dynamo mechanism can qualitatively affect the rotational evolution, collapse prospects, disk formation, and electromagnetic/multi-messenger signatures of long-lived binary neutron-star merger remnants, given that the positive-shear stably stratified core is not susceptible to the magnetorotational instability.
AI.method: Global, long-term general-relativistic neutrino-radiation magnetohydrodynamics simulations in axisymmetry, starting from a realistic merger remnant, with the unresolved Tayler-Spruit dynamo implemented via a newly developed mean-field dynamo subgrid prescription.
AI.result: The Tayler-Spruit dynamo is active mainly in high-latitude regions of the remnant core, producing Maxwell stresses that redistribute angular momentum on a few-hundred-millisecond spin-down timescale, substantially flattening the core rotation profile and transferring mass and AM to the disk, yielding a more massive, extended, strongly magnetized, low-electron-fraction disk and more neutron-rich ejecta.
AI.conclusion: The currently unmodelled Tayler-Spruit dynamo can qualitatively change the rotational evolution, collapse prospects, disk formation, and multi-messenger signatures of long-lived neutron-star merger remnants.

title: A Four-dimensional Model-agnostic Probe into the Astrophysical Origins of Binary Black Hole Subpopulations
summary: There is strong evidence of multiple binary black hole~(BBH) subpopulations in the cumulative gravitational wave catalog by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration that likely originate through distinct evolutionary channels. The astrophysical interpretation of this complex underlying population is subject to theoretical uncertainties in treatments of binary stellar evolution, core collapse, and host environments. Due to a lack of robust predictions and the sheer diversity of plausible features, strongly modelled population analyses often lead to prior-driven conclusions. On the other hand, flexible alternatives are often difficult to scale in higher dimensions, which can lead to a loss of critical information on astrophysically meaningful correlations. In this \textit{Letter}, we present the first data-driven reconstruction of the joint four-dimensional distribution of BBH primary masses, mass ratios, effective inspiral and effective precessing spin parameters, which yields novel model-agnostic constraints on the astrophysical origins of BBH subpopulations. We characterize four distinct subpopulations spanning different ranges of BBH masses and report new correlations in these specific mass ranges that are beyond the reach of strongly modeled parametrizations and lower-dimensional data-driven frameworks. Our results unveil novel insights into the abundances of specific subchannels of isolated binary evolution, dynamical assembly, and hierarchical mergers across various mass ranges in the astrophysical BBH population.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first data-driven reconstruction of the joint four-dimensional distribution of binary black hole primary masses, mass ratios, effective inspiral and effective precessing spin parameters using gravitational wave catalog data. It characterizes four distinct BBH subpopulations across different mass ranges and reveals new correlations beyond the reach of strongly modeled parametrizations and lower-dimensional data-driven frameworks, providing novel constraints on astrophysical origins including isolated binary evolution, dynamical assembly, and hierarchical mergers.
AI.motivation: Multiple BBH subpopulations exist in the gravitational wave catalog, but astrophysical interpretation is limited by theoretical uncertainties and prior-driven conclusions from strongly modeled analyses. Flexible alternatives struggle to scale to higher dimensions, losing information on astrophysically meaningful correlations. A model-agnostic, high-dimensional data-driven approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors perform the first data-driven reconstruction of the joint four-dimensional distribution of BBH properties: primary masses, mass ratios, effective inspiral spin, and effective precessing spin. This flexible high-dimensional approach avoids the prior dependence of strongly modeled parametrizations while retaining correlations across all four dimensions.
AI.result: The analysis characterizes four distinct BBH subpopulations spanning different mass ranges and reports new correlations in these specific mass ranges. The results unveil novel insights into the abundances of specific astrophysical subchannels including isolated binary evolution, dynamical assembly, and hierarchical mergers across various mass ranges.
AI.conclusion: The four-dimensional data-driven framework provides model-agnostic constraints on BBH subpopulations that go beyond what strongly modeled parametrizations and lower-dimensional flexible approaches can achieve, revealing new astrophysical insights into the formation channels of binary black holes.
